===PAGE 5=== (plain, 18 lines)
   1| In Memoriam
   2| John Francis Lattanzi was born to John and Frances (Lynch) Lattanzi on April 1, 1936, in Yonkers,
   3| New York. He grew up in Yonkers and Washington, New Jersey. In his youth John developed a life-
   4| long affinity for mischief, playing rousing piano by ear, and a love of outdoor pursuits. He graduated
   5| from Lafayette College in 1958, served as an officer in the U.S. Army, then embarked on a 30-year
   6| career with the American Can Company.
   7| He met his life-long partner, Christine Uhl, in 1961. They married, purchased a camp on Sebec Lake in
   8| Maine and started their family soon after. John and Christine raised their family in Cranford, NJ and
   9| Geneva, NY before moving to Lunenburg, MA in 1982.
  10| Over the past 43 years, John served his community in various roles on the Lunenburg Personnel Board,
  11| Conservation Commission, and Historical Society. John was a member of Saint Boniface and Our Lady
  12| of the Lake Churches, the Lunenburg Sportsman Club and the Sebec Lake Association.
  13| John leaves behind his beloved wife of over 61 years, and their five children; John Lattanzi Jr. and his
  14| wife Karen of Honolulu, HI; Jean Proctor and husband Dan of Lunenburg, MA; Peter Lattanzi and wife
  15| Dina of Cumberland, ME; Paul Lattanzi and wife AnnMarie or Yarmouth, ME; and James Lattanzi and
  16| wife Allison of Fitchburg, MA. John also leaves behind 15 grandchildren and his younger sister, Jane
  17| O’Connell, of Durham, NH.
  18| 1

===PAGE 6=== (plain, 19 lines)
   1| In Memoriam
   2|  Mario A. Patacchiola, 101, of Lunenburg formerly of Somerville, passed away on Wednesday, October 8, 2025
   3| in the Life Care Center of Leominster.
   4| Mario was born in Cambridge, on December 15, 1923, a son of the late Pasquale and Zelinda (Micille)
   5| Patacchiola. He graduated from Rindge High School in Cambridge and received his bachelor degree from
   6| Boston University.
   7| He worked for Bianchi Wedding Dress Company in Boston
   8| Mario was a WWII Veteran having served in U.S. Navy
   9| In 1955 Mario and his wife built a home on Hickory Hills Lake in Lunenburg and would summer there before
  10| making the move from Somerville to Lunenburg in 1985, and Dunnellon Fl. in the winter. His favorite activity
  11| was fishing and gardening in Lunenburg and Dunnellon .
  12| Mario was a faithful member of St. Boniface Parish and the Eagle House Senior Center, and a member of the
  13| American Legion and the AMVETS and Knights of Columbus
  14| His Wife of 79 years, Ann A. (Macone) Patacchiola passed away in 2023. He leaves two sons, Marc Patacchiola
  15| and his wife Gayle of Burlington and James Patacchiola and his wife Kathleen of Sterling; eight grandchildren,
  16| eleven great-grandchildren and several nephews and nieces.
  17| He is predeceased by his two sons, David Patacchiola in 2015 and Paul Patacchiola in 1990 + He had 5 brothers
  18| & sisters, Marco Marino Patacchiola, Helen Petrillo, Edward Patacchiola, Evelyn Rinaldo Walter Patacchiola
  19| 2

===PAGE 7=== (plain, 29 lines)
   1| In Memoriam
   2| Robert Joseph Saiia of Lunenburg, MA, affectionately known as Bob or Bobby, passed away peacefully on
   3| April 3, 2025, after a long battle with dementia. Bob was a loving husband to Donna and a devoted father to his
   4| daughter Tricia Back and son Michael Saiia.
   5| Born in Buffalo, New York (1944), Bob was proud of the days he spent working at The Bankers Life Insurance
   6| Company in Buffalo, NY~ later Principal Financial Group, where he was known for his dedication and hard
   7| work. As his career progressed, he was promoted and moved his family to Westerville, Ohio, where he became
   8| a proud Buckeye fan. His colleagues remember him as a kind and supportive mentor who always had a joke to
   9| share. He always held dear the memories of his days as a camp counselor at Camp Weona, just outside of
  10| Buffalo, NY. He also had a passion for coaching, whether it be his own children or once they were grown,
  11| volunteering as a football coach at Lunenburg High School. Bob also was very proud of the time he served on
  12| the Lunenburg Planning Board.
  13| Known as the life of the party, Bob valued every friendship, especially his lifelong friends from Frontier High
  14| School, where he graduated in 1962, affectionately calling themselves, HAAC-Hamburg Attitude Adjustment
  15| Club. Each and every friendship he made throughout his 81 years of life left an impact on him and he couldn’t
  16| go anywhere without making a new friend. His infectious laughter and warm spirit made him a beloved friend
  17| to all.
  18| Bob loved listening to Jazz, Frank Sinatra and Andrea Bocelli. He loved traveling to Italy and Europe with his
  19| wife Donna, but his favorite place to travel was Indiana where he could spend time with his children and
  20| grandchildren. He was the best Grandpa around to his two grandchildren, Renee and Anthony; they were his
  21| pride and joy and he would do just about anything to put a smile on their faces. He was always their biggest
  22| cheerleader and supporter and loved attending all their various events and activities. Bob adored his time with
  23| his family and his dogs, loved sports and he especially loved celebrating his Italian heritage. He took great pride
  24| in his roots and enjoyed sharing stories of his family's traditions and history.
  25| Bob is survived by his devoted wife, Donna Saiia, daughter Tricia Back (Robert Back), son Michael Saiia,
  26| grandchildren, Renee Back (19) and Anthony Back (18), stepchildren Christina Gallagher and Michael
  27| Gallagher, sister Kathy Krasowski, nieces Tracy Ensminger (Jeff Ensminger) and Julie Reinstein (Craig
  28| Reinstein), Linda Saiia Ross, and his five great nephews and one great niece.
  29| 3

===PAGE 8=== (plain, 12 lines)
   1| In Memoriam
   2| Elsa (Tocterman) Watson, 92, of Lunenburg died Wednesday, December 17, 2025 at University of
   3| Massachusetts – Memorial Hospital, Worcester.
   4| Her husband of 52 years, Herman S. Watson, died in May 2012.
   5| Elsa was born in Heilbronn, Germany, September 25, 1933 one of eight children born to Augen and Elsa
   6| (Wass) Tocterman and was educated in Germany. She moved to Lunenburg 62 years ago.
   7| For over twenty-five years Elsa worked independently as a home health aide in the area. She was a member of
   8| the Eastwood Club in Fitchburg and had been active in the activities at the Lunenburg and Townsend Senior
   9| Centers.
  10| She leaves her son and daughter in law, Rev. Jeffrey H. and Dina Watson of Sterling, MA and two grandsons,
  11| Jeffrey and Michael and Her sister Karin Tocterman in Germany.
  12| 4

===PAGE 9=== (layout, 38 lines)
   1|                                                  LUNENBURG PROFILE
   2|                                                YEAR                                                 INCORPORATED-1728
   3|                                                REGISTERED VOTERS– 9,240
   4|                                                      FY’25 TAX                                     RATE- $14.36
   5| OPEN TOWN GOVERNMENT– 5 MEMBER SELECT                              BOARD ANNUAL TOWN ELECTION– 3RD
   6| SATURDAY                                                                                                                                                                             IN MAY ANNUAL TOWN MEETING– 1ST SATURDAY                                                                       IN MAY TOTAL AREA– 26.63
   7| MILES
   8|   Lunenburg was settled in 1718 and                     incorporated in 1728. I         t occupies a   land area of   approximately 26.4
   9|   square miles. L unenburg is located in nort           h central   Massachusetts approximatel y 43 miles from       Bos-
  10|   ton, It i  s bordered on the west by the Town of Ashby and the City of Fitchburg, on the south by the
  11|   Town of Lancaster and the City of Leominster, on the east by the     Town of Shirley and on the north by
  12|   the Town of Townsend.
  13|   Local legislative decisions are made by an open town meeting.  Subjet to the legislative decisions
  14|   made by town meeting, the affairs of the town are generally administered by an elected five member
  15|   Select Board and a Town Manager and local school affairs are administered by an elected seven
  16|   member School Committee.
  17|   Lunenburg is a semi-rural community located in northern Worcester     County. Lake     Whalom and the for-
  18|   mer Whalom Amusement Park delineated the Whalom District from the remainder of Lunenburg. This
  19|   district was developed as a housing base for many factory workers working in the mills and factories of
  20|   Leominster and   Fitchburg. In many  ways  the characteristics of the     Whalom District closely reflect charac          -
  21|   teristics of  these c ities mor e t han of the rest of Lunenburg. The Hickory Hills L ake area w as    developed as
  22|   a private community co                   mprised largely of                          vacation cottages. Shirley Reservoir is a                                                             public water body         also
  23|   developed with mainly vacation cottages that have now been modified to year-round residences.
  24|   Commercial and industrial development is permitted in several areas of town, primarily along  the two
  25|   major arteries (Route 2A and 13) and the town's peripheries, due largely to the close proximity of
  26|   Leominster's and Fitchburg's sewer and water systems. Although many farms and orchards have slowly
  27|   developed into single family house, farming continues on in Lunenburg.  In 2013 the Annual Town
  28|   Meeting voted to establish an Agricultural Commission to represent, preserve and enhance farming in
  29|   the commujnity and to administer the "Right to Farm" bylaw.
  30|   In 2014 Lunenburg Town Meeting established the Architectural Preservation District ("District") bylaw
  31|   to regulate construction, demolition or renovation of existing "Contributing Property" structures as
  32|   defined  by the bylaw with an established bounded district.  The bylaw was introduced at Town Meeting
  33|   along with the Village District Bylaw, which created an overlay zoning district to encourage the
  34|   economic vitalization of downtown Lunenburg, the Architectural Preservation District Bylaw ensures
  35|   that it will not come at the expense of the town's historical character and integrity.
  36| Scan the QR Code to visit our website at https://www.lunenburgma.gov
  37| Follow us on Facebook at https://www.facebook.com/townoflunenburgma
  38| Follow us on Instagram at https://instagram.com/townoflunenburgma

===PAGE 20=== (layout, 46 lines)
   1|                                         REPORT OF THE TOWN MANAGER
   2|                                                             Fiscal Year 2025
   3| Fiscal Year 2025 saw                                                                                                                         significant transition            in the Office of the Town Manager.  The Office of the Town
   4| Manager was led by three individuals over the course of the year: Heather Lemieux, who departed in the
   5| summer of 2024 after eight years of dedicated service; Carter Terenzini, who served ably as Interim Town
   6| Manager from August 2024 through early February 2025; and Jennifer Warren-Dyment, who was appointed as
   7| Town Manager and began on February 4, 2025. Throughout these transitions, department heads, Town staff, the
   8| Select Board, and the many volunteers who serve on our boards and committees provided the continuity and
   9| commitment that kept Lunenburg moving forward.
  10| Below are the highlights of the key topics and accomplishments from FY25 within the Office of the Town
  11| Manager.
  12| Leadership Transition
  13| Town Manager Heather Lemieux submitted her notice to the Select Board in June of 2024.  Her last meeting
  14| with the Select Board was the evening of July 23, 2024, during which she offered heartfelt remarks on her
  15| service to the community.  She expressed gratitude to residents, board members, staff, business owners, and
  16| state officials, reflecting on her seven and a half years of service. She outlined major accomplishments,
  17| including long-term staffing plans for public safety, significant capital improvements, enhanced ADA
  18| accessibility, and infrastructure projects such as Complete Streets initiatives, Summer Street improvements, and
  19| bridge funding. She emphasized that her proudest achievements were the relationships built during her tenure.
  20| She clarified that her resignation was not requested by the Board and attributed her decision, in part, to a loss of
  21| trust. She concluded by thanking her family for their support and reiterated her commitment to having served
  22| Lunenburg with dedication and integrity.
  23| Carter Terenzini was engaged as Interim Town Manager beginning in August 2024. He brought extensive
  24| municipal management experience, including several prior engagements in the Interim role, and assumed the
  25| position immediately.  As Interim Town Manager, Mr. Terenzini not only kept the day-                       to-day operations
  26| running smoothly, but also advanced a number of capital projects, completed the obligation of ARPA funds,
  27| navigated multiple vacancies            , and made notable strides in improving employee engagement. At his final Select
  28| Board meeting on January 28, 2025, Interim Town Manager Terenzini presented his concluding report and was
  29| thanked by the Board for filling vacant positions, committing ARPA funds, and fostering greater employee
  30| participation during his tenure. Board members expressed appreciation for his work navigating challenging
  31| circumstances.
  32| With the Interim position filled, the Select Board stood up a Town Manager Screening Committee and hired the
  33| search firm of Community Paradigm Associates.  Per the Town Charter, The Town Manager shall be appointed
  34| by the Select Board from names submitted to it by a Town Manager Screening Committee which shall consist of
  35| 1 member of the Select Board, designated by it, 1 member of the School Committee, designated by it, 1 member
  36| of the planning board, designated by it, 1 member of the Finance Committee designated by it and the Town
  37| Moderator, who shall serve as the chair and call all meetings of the Town Manager Screening Committee.
  38| Whenever the position of Town Manager shall be vacant, the Town Manager Screening Committee shall be
  39| convened and shall solicit candidates, review applications, interview and rate candidates and submit the names
  40| of qualified candidates to the Select Board who shall appoint a Town Manager only from the names so
  41| prepared and submitted to it.
  42| The Screening Committee, Chaired by Town Moderator Tim Murphy, also included Tom Alonzo of the Select
  43| Board, Peter Beardmore of the School Committee, Chris Menard of the Finance Committee and Matt Brenner
  44| of the Planning Board.  The Committee                                                            worked with Community Paradigm to develop the Position Statement
  45| for the Town Manager Role, screen applications, interview semi-finalist candidates, and recommend a list of
  46| finalists to the Select Board for their consideration.  Much of the work of the Screening Committee is conducted

===PAGE 21=== (layout, 40 lines)
   1| in Executive Session.
   2| Three finalists were publicly interviewed by the Select Board on January 14, 2025.  They included Angeline
   3| Lopes Ellison, Jennifer Warren                                                                        -Dyment, and John Woodsmall.  The next evening, the Board moved (4-1) to
   4| appoint Ms. W           arren-Dyment as Town Manager pending successful negotiation. On January 28, 2025, the Select
   5| Board approved the contract with Ms. Warren                        -Dyment as Town Manager.              Ms. Warren            -Dyment began her first
   6| day on February 4, 2025, and began                                                             immediately engaging with department heads, the Select Board, and the
   7| budget process that was already well underway.
   8| Select Board Composition and Goals
   9| Throughout th           e majority of FY            25, the Select Board was composed of Chair Caesar Nuzzolo, Vice-                                            Chair
  10| Michael-Ray Jeffreys, Clerk Amanda Moore, Tom Alonzo, and Renee Emkey. The Board met regularly,
  11| typically the first three Tuesdays of the month, and addressed a wide range of Town business including the
  12| annual and special town meetings, policy updates, the Town Manager transition, budget discussions, licensing
  13| matters, and appointments.
  14| In the fall of 2024, the Select Board engaged in goal-setting discussions with Interim Town Manager Terenzini.
  15| The Board established the following goals (each goal including a number of additional objectives):
  16|      1)                                Establish policies in collaboration with the Town Manager and Assistant Town Manager/HR Director to
  17|           improve the quality of the Town as an employer, addressing the issues of recruitment, retention, and
  18|           overall work environment
  19|      2)                                Revamp the Select Board and Town Manager Goal-Setting Process
  20|      3)                                Increase Transparency and Availability of Information to the Public
  21|      4)                                Work through the Town Manager, Assistant Town Manager/HR Director and the department heads to
  22|           initially create, to periodically review and to develop and secure plans, policies and procedures
  23| Financial Matters
  24| FY26 Budget Development
  25| Interim Town Manager Terenzini began the FY26 budget process, working with the departments to develop
  26| budget request            s and                               with Finance Director/Town Accountant Ezequiel Ayala to develop revenue projections.
  27| Town Manager Warren-Dyment continued the FY26 budget process after her arrival. She held meetings with all
  28| departments in January and worked to understand the picture of revenues and expenditures and made initial
  29| revenue adjustments.
  30| By March 2025, the FY26 budget picture had come more fully            into sharper focus. The FY26 budget presented
  31| to the Select Board on March 19, 2025, included reductions across a number of areas, including cuts to the
  32| Pavement Management Plan (which were offset by Chapter 90 funding).
  33| On May 3, 2025, a $49,374,465,00 balanced budget was presented and approved at Town Meeting.  The budget
  34| was subsidized by a $500,000 appropriation of free cash to the Lunenburg Public Schools (LPS) to fund FY25
  35| and avoid an override allowing town and school leaders to have time to jointly plan for FY27.
  36| The need for additional state funding was a theme that persisted through the development of the FY26 budget
  37| with town and school leaders advocating for increased Chapter 70 and Unrestricted General Government Aid
  38| funding.
  39| Budget Task Force
  40| The Budget Task Force, formed by the Select Board, brought forward recommendations that were reviewed at

===PAGE 22=== (layout, 43 lines)
   1| the February 11, 2025 meeting.  The Task Force                                                                                                                     concluded there were three structural causes to the state of
   2| disrepair in Lunenburg: 1) Proposition 2 ½ funding; 2) lack of competitive employment packages; and 3) an
   3| overly complex financial structure for the town.
   4| Recommendations of the Task Force included 1) consolidating town investment accounts and funds; 2) a
   5| targeted diagnostic audit; 3) implement the prudent investment rule                                   ; 4) review the viability of the Community
   6| Preservation Act; 5) Green grants for HVACs; 6) solar on old town dump; 7) solar on school lots; 8) Brooks
   7| House lease; 9) review trash and recycling programs; 10) designate additional roads as town roads; 11)
   8| implement a high deductible health plan; 12) increase health insurance opt outs; 13) payroll and purchase order
   9| streamlining; 14) standardize and improve workflow for town finances; 15) review school solar contracts; 16)
  10| create regular review process for school fees; 17) create regular review process for town fees; 18) change
  11| warrant delivery; 19) consolidate town and school snow removal and ground maintenance; and 20) determine
  12| viability of split tax rate.
  13| Other Financial Mentions
  14| Town Manager Lemieux had obtained a grant to work with the Division of Local Services (DLS) to draft an
  15| update Lunenburg’s financial policies and procedures which were not adopted prior to her departure.  Interim
  16| Town Manager Terenzini shared the draft             and encouraged feedback and commentary.  This project was not
  17| completed in FY25.
  18| As of March 2025, the Town had received over $225,000 in cumulative opioid settlement funds. Town Manager
  19| Warren-Dyment began preliminary discussions with the Police Chief and Fire Chief on the potential use of
  20| these funds.  No funds were expended in FY25.
  21| A final tax rate of $14.36 per thousand was established for FY25.  Free cash was certified at $2,270,060.
  22| Infrastructure, Facilities, and Capital Projects
  23| Flat Hill Road Bridge
  24| The Flat Hill Road Bridge replacement over Catacoonamug Brook was the most significant and most
  25| challenging capital project of FY2025. After years of planning, the project, funded by a previously secured
  26| $500,000 Small Bridge Grant and supplemental MassDOT funding, was awarded to Kenefick Corporation. The
  27| road was closed beginning March 7, 2025, with an anticipated reopening of April 25, 2025 and a detour route
  28| put in place and communicated widely to the public.  However, the water level in the lake had already risen
  29| significantly by the time work was to begin, and Kenefick’s water control plan proved inadequate for the
  30| conditions. No work was performed on the structure, and Kenefick submitted a request for a one-year extension,
  31| which was denied.  The bridge remained closed for the remainder of FY25 after a MassDOT Underwater Bridge
  32| Inspection Team inspection found additional section in the structure.
  33| Town Building Projects
  34|     •                                                 The Town Hall Roof Replacement and Chimney Restoration project was one of the major capital
  35|          investments of FY25. The contract was issued in December 2024 under Interim Town Manager
  36|          Terenzini, with the chimneys prioritized first as they were anticipated to generate the most change
  37|          orders. Winter weather slowed progress, but by March 2025 both Town Hall chimneys were complete
  38|          and the roofing work had begun. By April 2025 the Town Hall roof was nearly complete. The contractor
  39|          then transitioned to the Ritter Memorial Building, completing chimney repointing, flashing repairs, slate
  40|          tile replacement, and gutter and trim work. The project was substantially complete by May 2025.
  41|     •                                                 The Library Teen Room expansion was completed during FY25. The project included construction of
  42|          two new offices (Phase 1), expansion of the teen room itself (Phase 2), and replacement of the children’s
  43|          story craft room floor.

===PAGE 23=== (layout, 44 lines)
   1|      •                                                           The Adult Activity Center kitchen renovation, a long-delayed FY21 capital project, was completed
   2|           during FY25. The renovation included a new stove, warming oven, stainless sink, stainless counters, and
   3|           a grease trap installation. A rotted sub-slab drain pipe was discovered during construction and repaired,
   4|           delaying the kitchen’s reopening, but the kitchen was back in full use by May 2025.
   5|      •                                                           A $185,000 Townwide Keying and Security project was included in the FY25 Capital Plan to replace all
   6|           exterior locks and upgrade access control systems at Town Hall, the Ritter Memorial Building, the
   7|           Public Safety Building, the Adult Activity Center, the Library, the DPW facility, the Beach House, and
   8|           the Teen Center. A contract with Dugmore and Duncan was executed in the Spring of 2025, but the
   9|           project was not completed within the Fiscal Year.
  10|      •                                                           The DPW Floor Project and DPW Roof Project both commenced in December 2024.
  11|      •                                                           The Senior Center Roof project was completed in the fall of 2024.
  12| ARPA Fund Obligations
  13| Completing the obligation of all American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds before the federal deadline was one
  14| of Interim Town Manager Terenzini’s most urgent and consequential priorities during FY2025. The Town had
  15| received approximately $3.5 million in ARPA Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds (SLFRF),
  16| and the federal requirement had evolved from a definition of “committed” funds to requiring that all dollars be
  17| under contract by December 31, 2024. This created a compressed and challenging timeline.
  18| The ARPA-funded project portfolio being moved to contract during FY25 included a wide range of municipal
  19| investments including supplementing existing projects on prior year capital plans as well as additional facilities
  20| and infrastructure side projects            , public safety upgrades, school projects, Water District projects, software
  21| upgrades, and funding for community programs.
  22| By the end of December, all funds were obligated.  When Interim Town Manager Terenzini presented his final
  23| report to the Select Board on January 28, 2025, he cited the successful commitment of ARPA funds as one of
  24| the signature accomplishments of his tenure. Chair Nuzzolo drafted a press release to communicate to the
  25| public the full scope of ARPA investments the Town had made on behalf of the community.
  26| Personnel
  27| Staffing remained an ongoing challenge and priority throughout FY25. Key staffing actions during FY25
  28| included: the completion of the Police Chief search and appointment; continued recruitment of the Land Use
  29| Director; the search and recruitment of the Senior Center Director; the filling of the Assistant to the Sewer
  30| Business Manager position; the recruitment for the Conservation Agent; a vacancy in the position of Executive
  31| Assistant to the Town Manager and Select Board to name a few.
  32| One of the most significant recruitments of             FY25 was the search for a new Police Chief following Chief
  33| Thomas Gammel’s retirement. Applications for the Police Chief position closed in early February 2025. A
  34| Screening Committee comprised of the Fire Chief, COA Director, Superintendent, a Chief from another
  35| community, a Town Manager from another community, and Town Manager Warren-Dyment reviewed all
  36| applications and conducted interviews on March 12, 2025. Promoted from Lieutenant and then Interim Chief,
  37| Jeffrey Thibodeau, was sworn in as Lunenburg’s Police Chief at a well            -attended swearing            -in and pinning
  38| ceremony held on April 18, 2025.  Select Board Chair Caesar Nuzzolo served as Master of Ceremonies                                                                                                                                                                                                             and
  39| PACC produced a video of the ceremony for those unable to attend in person.
  40| After 30 years of service, Sue Doherty retired as COA Director on December 31, 2024.  After a recruitment
  41| process, Deb Goodsell was hired to take over the helm at the Center.  Deb brought significant experience to the
  42| position, having served in Clinton                                    for ten years as their Director.
  43| After a sustained vacancy in the role of Land Use Director that was vacated by Adam Burney, Christopher
  44| Reilly was hired in September             2024. The position was vacated again in April 2025 and recruitment continued

===PAGE 24=== (layout, 35 lines)
   1| for the duration of FY25.
   2| Community
   3| The Town of Lunenburg celebrated several meaningful community milestones during FY 2025. The swearing-
   4| in ceremony for new Police Chief Thibodeau in April 2025 was a widely attended and celebratory event. The
   5| Agricultural Commission hosted a well-received agricultural fair at the TC Passios grounds in October 2024.
   6| The Lunenburg Vendor Fair, organized by the Lunenburg Business Association and Parks Department, was
   7| held for the first time on May 10, 2025, at TC Passios                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     and featured a number of vendors, food trucks, live
   8| music, a petting zoo, and other activities.
   9| Through volunteer efforts, a bocce court was installed at the Adult Activity Center and                         was completed in
  10| roughly an hour and a half in the Fall of 2024, with Facilities Director Chris Ruth coordinating the effort.  In
  11| April 2025, the Council on Aging and the Town celebrated Charles Sanderson, World War II veteran and
  12| remarkable 101-year-old Lunenburg resident, with a presentation of the Boston Post Cane and a formal
  13| welcome to the Century Club.
  14| Closing Remarks
  15| Fiscal Year 2025 was a year that asked much of the Town of Lunenburg and of everyone who serves it.
  16| Through a leadership transition that spanned three managers and the loss of transfer of knowledge that goes
  17| with such a transition, an activelist of c                                            apital projects in various stages, continued budgetary pressures, and the
  18| ongoing work of keeping a community running, the Town’s staff, elected and appointed officials, and
  19| volunteers continued to show up with dedication and care.
  20| Thank you to the members of the Select Board that served in FY25: Caesar Nuzzolo, Michael                                                                         -Ray Jeffreys,
  21| Amanda Moore, Tom Alonzo, Renee Emkey, Brian Lehtinen, and Glenn McLeod for the leadership,
  22| engagement, and collaboration.
  23| Thank you to all department heads who have served for the continuity and leadership which provided stability
  24| throughout the year.  Thank you to the staff that work in all of our departments for the work that you do.  You
  25| are our unsung heroes                                                                                     that keep the operations of the town going.
  26| And thank you to the many volunteers who serve on Lunenburg’s boards, committees, and commissions.  A few
  27| special thank you to those who assisted in the transition of not only town leadership, but also transitions within
  28| their departmental areas: Matt Brenner, Planning Board Chair; Chris Menard, Finance Committee Char; and
  29| Karin Menard, Parks Commission Chair.
  30| Most importantly- to the residents and businesses who make Lunenburg a community worth serving every day-
  31| thank you.
  32| Respectfully submitted,
  33| Jennifer Warren-Dyment
  34| Town Manager,
  35| Town of Lunenburg

   5| Under the umbrella of Massachusetts state and local town laws, Lunenburg's Assessing Organization will work
   6| with town operations and our citizens to meet our vision for delivering a fair and equitable taxation.  The
   7| Lunenburg Board of Assessors will evolve and administer a series of “Best Practices” methodologies consistent
   8| with our Vision. These practices will ensure equitable treatment and compassion for all of our citizens.
   9| The Boar d of Assessors has empowered an Assessor Organization that has the capability to evaluate and assess
  10| all property at its full and fair market value.  This is accomplished through a rigorous measurement of property,
  11| collection of appropriate data, analysis and maintenance of all property tax data records. Additionally, the
  12| Assessor Department administers a motor vehicle excise tax, real estate and motor vehicle tax abatements, and
  13| all statutory tax exemptions as allowed by law. The Assessor Organization will work cohesively with other
  14| town departments.
  15| The last year has seen a lot of progress in restoring the fully functional Assessors’ Office.
  16|          •                                                 We continue to be fully staffed after several years of being understaffed. Our staff includes a full time
  17|                    Principal Assessor, a 19-hour Data Collector and a 32-hour Assessing Administrative Assistant.
  18|          •                                                 The Assessing office and files have been reorganized from the disarray in 2023.
  19|          •                                                 Assessing Policies and Procedures have been established.
  20|          •                                                 A sales inspection program has been established to follow-up on sales and review property data in MLS.
  21|                    Permit inspections are conducted weekly and a cyclical program has been established with the
  22|                    inspection of over 500 properties annually to comply with the DOR Directives from the 2024
  23|                    revaluation.
  24|          •                                                 We successfully improved several exemptions by loosening eligibility income and asset limits
  25|                    qualification for Seniors and increasing exemptions amounts.  We also worked on developing a new
  26|                    “Senior Means Tested Tax Exemption” for implementation in the fall of 2025 (FY2026).
  27| The Board of Assessors’ efforts at restoring the trust of Lunenburg taxpayers include scheduling all our
  28| meetings during evenings (with both PACC coverage and Zoom access) so everyone can participate more
  29| easily.  The Board has also developed a Property Tax program for use at the Senior Center and has held a yearly
  30| senior tax exemption presentation to create awareness of the available real estate tax exemptions for the seniors.
  31| We continue to improve visibility and access by redesigning of the Website, including analytics and
  32| explanations provided the Massachusetts DOR / Division of Local Services, Massachusetts Association of
  33| Assessing Officers, and UMass among others.  The office staff strives to provide exceptional service that the
  34| Lunenburg taxpayers deserve.

  14| The Town of Lunenburg Building Department is Located in the Ritter Memorial Building located at 960
  15| Massachusetts Avenue. The Building Department works to efficiently, effectively, and consistently ensure a
  16| safe, sustainable, and vibrant community through effective oversight of construction and development activities
  17| by enforcing the Massachusetts state Building, Plumbing, Gas, and Electrical Codes, The Architectural Access
  18| Board Regulations, and Lunenburg’s Zoning Bylaw and Town Code. The Building Department also plays a
  19| critical role in assisting business through the process of obtaining permits and ensuring compliance with all
  20| relevant codes and regulations. A commitment to being accessible, responsive and to providing a high level of
  21| customer service empowers us to be a partner the community, property owners, businesses, contractors, and
  22| developers can rely on when needed. The Building Department maintains this commitment by:
  23|      •                                                 Ensuring the public has consistent access to effective and courteous assistance in obtaining information,
  24|           permits or approvals related to construction, building or zoning regulations and providing clear
  25|           information about regulations, permitting requirements and associated fees.
  26|      •                                                 Maintaining a consistent level of communication by responding to all inquiries and applications in a
  27|           timely manner.
  28|      •                                                 Enforcing building codes, regulations, local codes, and safety standards to
  29|           guarantee the safety of occupants and the community.
  30|      •                                                 Improving and optimizing the permitting process to facilitate efficient and timely approvals for
  31|           construction projects while maintaining thorough and consistent review procedures.
  32|      •                                                 Utilizing technology to streamline internal processes, enhance data management, and provide better
  33|           online services for applicants and property owners.
  34|      •                                                 Regularly reviewing and assessing departmental processes and policies, seeking opportunities for
  35|           improvement, efficiency, and effectiveness in serving the community.
  36|      •                                                 Coordinating with other departments to ensure a streamlined approach to permitting and enforcement as
  37|           needed.
  38|      •                                                   Receiving and evaluating feedback from the public and other interested parties, and implementing
  39|           changes as needed to ensure the department goals are being met.
  40|      •

  10|                                                         CEMETERY COMMISION
  11| Throughout the past year, the Cemetery Commission met regularly with DPW Director William Bernard and
  12| Cemetery Superintendent Todd Holman to review day‑to‑day operations, maintenance needs, and long‑term
  13| planning for Lunenburg’s public burial grounds. The Commission also conducted several on‑site visits to North,
  14| South, and Fish Street Cemeteries to assess current conditions and identify upcoming needs.
  15| The Cemetery Commission is an elected three‑member board with staggered three‑year terms. Its
  16| responsibilities include establishing cemetery regulations, overseeing care and management of public burial
  17| grounds, and laying out lots and pathways in both existing and newly acquired cemetery land. Daily operations
  18| are handled by the Town Manager and delegated to the DPW Director, as the Cemetery Division operates
  19| within the Department of Public Works.
  20| Overview of Cemetery Properties
  21|      •                                                           North Cemetery (Holman Street)
  22|            Approximately 22 acres, with about 10 currently active. The property includes open land suitable for
  23|            near‑term expansion and additional wooded areas for long‑term development.  23-                                                                                   acre wetlands parcel
  24|            also borders the site.
  25|      •                                                           South Cemetery (Page Street)
  26|            About 6 active acres, with limited remaining expansion capability.
  27|      •                                                           Fish Street Cemetery (Fish & Lincoln Streets) – Goodrich Family
  28|            A historic 0.06‑acre family plot with five marked graves and additional identified burial locations.
  29|      •                                                           West Street Terrace – Arnold, Litch, & Moulten Families
  30|            A small historic family cemetery located on private property.
  31| Both North and South Cemeteries remain open for lot sales and burials.
  32| Projects and Improvements
  33| Significant progress was made on the North Cemetery backlot expansion this year. Town Meeting appropriated
  34| $50,000 in May 2025, and the Commission contracted with Dillis & Roy for engineering services. Preliminary
  35| plans were submitted.  The bidding process for construction will be in Fiscal Year 2026.
  36| Administrative improvements included purchasing a secure file cabinet for cemetery records and continuing
  37| support for the CIMS software system, which offers digital mapping, ownership records, and public search
  38| tools.
  39| Maintenance efforts included:
  40|      •                                                           Rebuilding roughly 150 feet of stone wall, completed by Amanda Construction at the South Cemetery.
  41|      •                                                           New concrete pad for flag poles at the South Cemetery, completed by Mike McAllister.
  42|      •                                                           Installation of 20 new cedar trees to replace aging hedges by Lakeview Landscaping at the North

   1|              Cemetery.
   2|       •                                                           Roadside trimming by Ray Morin and front hedge work by Beaulac Brothers
   3|       •                                                           Roadway crack sealing by Indus, Inc at both North and South Cemeteries.
   4| All work was performed under the supervision of the Cemetery Superintendent.

  23|                                                      CONSERVATION
  24| The Town of Lunenburg Conservation Commission is a seven-member commission, each appointed to 3-year
  25| terms by the Select Board, whose duties are codified under the Conservation Commission Act MGL chapter 40
  26| s 8C. The Commission enforces the Massachusetts Wetland Protection Act MGL chapter 131 s 40 and Chapter
  27| 239 of the local bylaws for the protection of wetlands.  The Commission also manages, and controls town
  28| owned lands retained for conservation and passive recreation use.
  29| The fiscal year 2025-26 was a very busy and active agenda containing both public hearings and meetings for a
  30| wide range of projects from commercial development, subdivisions and small single family upkeep projects and
  31| larger scale industrial/commercial proposals.  The Commission also held numerous inspections on weekends
  32| prior to meetings to familiarize themselves with the upcoming proposals that would appear on the agenda.
  33| During this period the Conservation Commission supported 28 NOIs, 36 Administrative Determinations, 18
  34| RDAs, 34 COCs, and numerous other requests.
  35| The Conservation Commission continues to implement forest stewardship plans developed using grants as
  36| outlined in the last annual reports. The funding from the sale of harvested timber provides the seed money to
  37| make it possible for the Commission to apply for grants to maintain and improve Lunenburg’s Conservation
  38| Lands. The Conservation Commission continues to execute on the awarded MASS Recreational Trail Program
  39| Grant that was awarded in 2023. The purpose of this grant was to fund the engineering design and permitting
  40| work to create parking access in Table Rock and Rayno Conservation Areas. The grant scope also covered
  41| improving Accessible Access to the Cowdrey Conservation Area as accessed from Townsend Harbor Road. In
  42| early 2025, the permits were issued for Table Rock and Rayno Areas. This effort is ongoing to complete the
  43| engineering design and permitting work in the Cowdrey. Members of the commission applied for two additional
  44| grants for the upcoming year.

===PAGE 47=== (plain, 39 lines)
   1| The Pollinator Habitat portion of the Hollis Rd property provides for a diversity of native flowers throughout
   2| the growing season. The Habitat promotes insect egg laying and nesting sites for pollinators. The Habitat
   3| provides food sources for birds and numerous insects including native bees and butterflies. This unique “Hidden
   4| Gem” works as an ambassador for native pollinators to our community. We are very thankful for the dedicated
   5| volunteers supporting the Lunenburg Community Pollinator Habitat.
   6| The Conservation Commission will sponsor April Earth Day projects across Conservation Properties. The
   7| Commission would like to express our gratitude for all the hard-working volunteers that work so
   8| enthusiastically in maintaining and improving Lunenburg’s conservation lands!
   9| The Commission has also continued to work closely with Lake Shirley and Hickory Hills on the implementation
  10| of their lake management plans.  These plans set goals and action items designed to give a better picture of the
  11| overall health of the lakes and define various strategies to ensure continued protection of these valuable
  12| resources. Both lakes presented to the commission in early 2026.
  13| The administrative office position was removed from the Clerical Union at Town Meeting and moved to SAP
  14| with a new title of Conservation Agent. This helped the office attract and extremely qualified full-time agent
  15| and the Commission looks forward to full time office support.
  16| The Commission thanks all the town agencies for their continued support!

  22| COUNCIL ON AGING
  23| The mission of the Council on Aging is to advocate for the improved quality of life for all residents age 50+
  24| through supportive services, programs, and education. Councils on Aging were established under Massachusetts
  25| General Law Chapter 40, section 8B, to include setting policy for the administration of elder programs or
  26| services and to develop, coordinate, and conduct such activities which advocate for this population’s issues.
  27| The FY25 Council on Aging staff consisted of Susan Doherty/Debra Goodsell, Director; Michele Beauvais,
  28| Administrative Assistant and Transportation; Pauline Roy, Outreach Coordinator; Pamela Myllykangas, Meal
  29| Site Coordinator; Sandra Ricci, Asst. Meal Site Coordinator; Elsa Watson and Ann Penney, Meal Site
  30| Assistants; Jim McGuigan, David Gallagher, & Kimberly Moore, MART Van Drivers.
  31| The Council on Aging Board is an eleven-member board appointed to 3-year terms by the Lunenburg Select
  32| Board. The FY24 Council on Aging Board members were Chairperson Deb Lincoln, Vice-Chairperson Jane
  33| Rabbitt, Ana Lockwood, Pete Lincoln/Jack Rabbitt, Jim McGuigan, Diane Nowd, Cathy Beale, Susan
  34| O’Sullivan, Elena Christopher, Judith Tarbell/Lou Franco & Helen Balcom.
  35| The Town budget alone does not support the Lunenburg COA at the Lunenburg Adult Activity Center. Other
  36| sources of funding include the Eagle House Supporters Inc., a non-profit 501c3 group, Formula Grant funding
  37| from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, and Montachusett Regional Transit Authority.
  38| In FY23 the Eagle House Senior Community Center rebranded its name to the Lunenburg Adult Activity
  39| 43

===PAGE 48=== (layout, 39 lines)
   1| Center. The change has encouraged all people aged 50+ to visit the center and participate in programming.
   2| FY25 showed a continued increase in the number of daily participants.  Growth is anticipated through 2050.
   3| Construction was completed on a new commercial kitchen in the Spring of 2025 using funds that had been
   4| previously allocated to this project.
   5| We are incredibly lucky to have a large volunteer force at the Council on Aging. In FY25, we had forty-two
   6| (42) volunteers who contributed 668 hours of their time to help us out in various ways, such as driving for the
   7| Meals on Wheels program, program leaders, kitchen helpers, Memory Café, office help, library, handyman, and
   8| friendly visitors/phone calls. We greatly appreciate their service.
   9| In FY25, we offered a variety of programs including Meals on Wheels, congregate lunches and breakfast
  10| programs, transportation, health and wellness, arts and crafts, bocce, cards, and games, cultural, Veterans
  11| Breakfast, movies, Historical Society presentations, information and referral, Memory Café, health insurance
  12| counseling, and social events both at the Adult Activity Center and offsite to individuals age 50+.
  13| There were approximately 1184 people who utilized the Adult Activity Center in FY25. Those 1184 people
  14| compiled 22,871 units of duplicated service by participating in the programs listed above.
  15| The Lunenburg Council on Aging newsletter lists current events and is available for you online at
  16| www.mycommunityonline.com , or you can pick up a copy at the Lunenburg Adult Activity Center, Town Hall,
  17| Library, Post Office, local churches, and various businesses throughout the community.

  31|                                        DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
  32| The Department of Public Works is honored to serve the residents of Lunenburg each day. Our work touches
  33| nearly every part of community life—from safe roads and reliable sewer services to well                                                -maintained cemeteries
  34| and a clean environment. The DPW is made up of the Highway, Cemetery, Sewer, and Vehicle Maintenance
  35| Divisions, all supported by a dedicated team of public works professionals who take great pride in caring for
  36| our town.
  37| Our staff includes one Director, one Executive Assistant (shared with Facilities), one Highway Superintendent,
  38| three Heavy Equipment Operators, two Driver/Laborers, one Mechanic, one Cemetery Superintendent, two
  39| Seasonal Cemetery Laborers, one Sewer Business Manager, and one Assistant to the Sewer Business Manager.

  22| Highway Division

  10| Bridges and Culverts
  11| In 2025, we completed a Bridge Assessment and Ranking Plan, outlining prioritized repairs for six bridges and
  12| culverts. This plan helps the Town coordinate future work efficiently and submit stronger applications for state
  13| and federal funding.
  14| Tree Removal and Vegetation Care
  15| Lunenburg’s roadside trees are a cherished part of our landscape, but they also require ongoing attention. The
  16| DPW continues to manage tree hazards using the 2015 Tree Risk Management Inventory as a guide, while also
  17| responding to new issues caused by aging trees and severe storms.
  18| Because we lack specialized equipment such as a bucket truck or crane, larger removals are outsourced. We are
  19| grateful to Unitil for their continued partnership in removing hazardous trees that threaten power lines.
  20| Our team also expanded roadside vegetation clearing using our utility tractor and boom mower and is
  21| developing a more comprehensive town-wide mowing plan for the future.
  22| Landfill and Environmental Stewardship
  23| The capped landfill on Youngs Road remains in compliance with MassDEP requirements. A consultant
  24| performs gas and groundwater testing, while the DPW monitors the site and contracts out mowing.
  25| Adjacent to the landfill, we responsibly store catch basin materials and sweeping debris under a state-approved
  26| Beneficial Use Determination (BUD) permit.
  27| We also continued hosting Yard Waste Days                                     on seven Saturdays in the fall and seven in the spring, giving
  28| residents a convenient opportunity to dispose of brush and leaves for composting.
  29| Solid Waste and Recycling
  30| In 2025, the Town welcomed GW Shaw and Son as our new trash and recycling contractor, following many
  31| years of service from E.L. Harvey & Sons.
  32| Weekly collection continued under the Pay-As-You-Throw (PAYT) program, with PAYT bags available at
  33| various local businesses.
  34| Residents also have access to:
  35|      •                                                     Household hazardous waste disposal at the Devens facility
  36|      •                                                     Additional fee-based recycling at the CHARM Center in Townsend
  37| The DPW remains the primary contact for residents with trash and recycling questions.

  13|                                                    FINANCE COMMITTEE
  14| On May 3, 2025, members of the public gathered in the Lunenburg Middle/High School and participate in the
  15| centuries-long tradition of New England style town government. As part of this tradition, the Finance
  16| Committee has reviewed all monied articles, recommended updates, held public hearings, and has voted on our
  17| official recommendations. This warrant contains five budgetary articles that are worth highlighting:
  18|     •                                           Article 10: Omnibus Budget article that provides most funds for the operations of town (both municipal
  19|          and schools).
  20|     •                                           Article 12: One-time, free cash funding to the School Department, breaking from Lunenburg’s
  21|          traditional practices but potentially necessary to fund essential school services.
  22|     •                                           Article 11: A Citizens Petition requesting a Proposition 2 ½ override of $2,099,337.
  23|     •                                           Article 28: A Debt Exclusion article requesting $13.8M in bonds for construction and revitalization
  24|          following Master Plan of Marshall Park.
  25|     •                                           Article 29: A Debt Exclusion Article requesting between $21,409,100 and $22,301,145 in bonds to
  26|          renovate Town Hall into a Meeting House, renovate Ritter Memorial, and add a Town Hall addition onto
  27|          Ritter Memorial.
  28| The first three articles are related to operational budgets and service levels for the Town. This report will
  29| summarize the impact on planned operations, and detailed presentations will be given at Town Meeting. The
  30| last two articles are debt exclusion articles resulting from years of planning and design work by two
  31| commissions.
  32| Town Revenue Projections
  33| Lunenburg’s revenue comes from multiple sources, primarily Property Tax. This year’s budget builds on the
  34| FY25 Levy Limit of $31,602,108, including increases from the successful FY25 Proposition 2 ½ override. By
  35| law, the levy limit increases automatically by 2.5%, resulting in an increase of $790,052.70. Additionally, the
  36| Town estimates new growth of $400,000, leading to a total increase of 3.76%. Previously approved excluded
  37| debt of $2,213,677 is then applied, resulting in a maximum allowable levy of $35,005,838.
  38| FY2026 Net State Aid is estimated at $10,006,739, based on the Governor's budget, with potential increases
  39| pending State Legislator’s negotiations. Chapter 70 Governor’s budget is set at $9,109,185, reflecting ongoing
  40| challenges with state aid for education. The Chapter 70 program is the primary source of state aid for funding

===PAGE 53=== (layout, 41 lines)
   1| local public elementary and secondary schools. From FY13                        -FY23 state aid increased at an annual rate of 5.3%,
   2| but in the last three years, it has slowed to 1.5%, increasing the financial burden on the town to raise and
   3| appropriate funds. From a Lunenburg resident’s perspective, State Aid is funded through income and sales
   4| taxes.

  21| Additional revenue sources include local receipts (Excise Tax, Meals Tax, etc.) and enterprise funds such as
  22| Sewer. Notably, Chapter 90 funding for municipal capital improvements has increased from $418,227 to
  23| $690,000 due to a five-     year state-level bond bill.
  24| Operations
  25| Many Town Meeting articles relate to operational budgets. Lunenburg, like most municipalities in the
  26| Commonwealth, faces increased health insurance costs (14.84% increase), stagnant state aid, necessary salary
  27| increases to remain competitive, and inflation. As a result, the vast majority of department staffing plans have
  28| been maintained, placed on hold, or reduced. The Fire Department and School Department experienced the
  29| most significant impacts of these decisions this year, though all departments were affected.
  30| School Department Operations
  31| The School Committee and Superintendent have aligned their budget with the Town Manager’s plan,
  32| representing $25,787,474 in the Omnibus Budget. While grants augment this budget, Town Meeting voters
  33| determine omnibus budget funding. This budget necessitates eliminating approximately 28 Full-Time
  34| Equivalents (39 employees) at the time of writing this report.
  35| A Citizens Petition article for $2,099,337 aims to restore level funding to FY25 operations. As of this report, the
  36| Finance Committee has not received details of this article. The Select Board voted unanimously to recommend
  37| disapproval of this article and further voted to not include the Proposition 2 ½ override on the Annual Town
  38| Election Warrant. The Finance Committee also voted unanimously to recommend disapproval of this article.
  39| As a Proposition 2 ½ override the article would require passage at Town Meeting and at an Election, therefor no
  40| path exists for this article.
  41| If approved, the Tax Rate would increase by approximately $0.89 per $1,000 of property value, translating to an

===PAGE 54=== (layout, 41 lines)
   1| average annual increase of $449 for a single-family household valued at $504,937.  This is a 6.19% increase in
   2| property tax.
   3| If the override is rejected, Article 12             proposes a $500,000 Free Cash transfer to the School Department as a
   4| temporary measure to delay service cuts. The School Committee has not yet determined how these funds would
   5| be allocated, with further details expected at Annual Town Meeting.
   6| Fire Department Operations
   7| The Fire Department currently operates three shifts covering 24/7 town operations, leading to a 48-hour, six-
   8| day-per-week schedule. Sundays are covered by call and per-diem staff, with 62% of coverage provided by
   9| career firefighters. Of the 197 Massachusetts Fire Departments providing 24/7 coverage, Lunenburg is one of
  10| only six operating with three shifts. Most departments use a four-shift model, making Lunenburg less
  11| competitive in hiring and retention. The shift expansion plan remains on hold for another year.
  12| Borrowing
  13| The town employs two types of borrowing:
  14|      •                                                     Regular Debt, typically for smaller projects within the Tax Levy Limit.
  15|      •                                                     Excludable Debt, requiring Town Meeting and ballot approval, which does not permanently increase
  16|           taxes—once the debt is repaid, the tax rate decreases.
  17| According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, “Municipal debt is an important tool for city and
  18| town governments to finance the purchase of expensive capital assets and to construct and maintain municipally
  19| owned infrastructure.  However, debt cannot become overburdensome to either the community’s property tax
  20| paying population or to the budget. Capital purchasing and/or improvements should ideally be planned with its
  21| priorities analyzed and reviewed by a capital planning committee seeking to coordinate community planning
  22| with debt affordability and aiming to present its recommendations to municipal leaders and to the public.”
  23| The Town policy states that:
  24|      •                                                     Principal and Interest on Regular Debt remain below 4%.
  25|      •                                                     Excludable Debt remains below 11%.
  26|      •                                                     Combined debt remains below 14%.
  27| This year, Regular Debt decreases by $393,881.14, with these funds being utilized for:
  28|      1.                                    FY26 Capital Program ($244,576)
  29|      2.                                    Operating Budget Offsets ($149,305)
  30| Two debt-funded projects are on the Warrant and Ballot:
  31|      1.                                    Marshall Park improvements ($13.8M via Excludable Debt)
  32|      2.                                    Municipal Building renovations ($21.4M - $22.3M via Excludable Debt)
  33| Marshall Park Improvements ($13.8M via Excludable Debt): Require full funding approval before pursuing
  34| grants exceeding $1.5M. The Parks Commission has been encouraged to reapply for prior high-scoring grants
  35| such as PARC and Land and Water that scored highly. The Parks Commission was successful in securing
  36| Grants in excess of $1.5M prior to the project being put on hold in 2024.   As presented for the Marshall Park
  37| project, the Tax Levy would increase by approximately $0.46 per $1,000 on top of the FY26 increase. The
  38| average single-family household has a valuation of $504,937 and would result in an increase of $231 per year in
  39| taxes. This is a 3.2% increase in property tax.
  40| Municipal Building Renovations ($21.4M - $22.3M via Excludable Debt): As presented for the Municipal
  41| Building project the Tax Levy would increase by approximately $0.57 per $1,000 on top of the FY26 increase.

===PAGE 55=== (layout, 34 lines)
   1| The average single-family household has a valuation of $504,937 and would result in an increase of $288 per
   2| year in taxes. This is a 3.97% increase in property tax.
   3| The estimated tax impact for the Marshall Park and Municipal Building projects will be detailed at Town
   4| Meeting.  Both projects combined would remain under the Combined debt policy limit of 14%.  The combined
   5| projects would be around the 11% excludable debt policy limit.

  25| A Year of Stewardship, Renewal, and Community Connection
  26| As Library Director, it is my pleasure to present this year’s annual report on the activities of the Lunenburg
  27| Public Library. After years of serving rural communities, I can say with confidence that what we have
  28| accomplished together this year is something special. Our library continues to be a true gem in the town—not
  29| only a place of books, but a living, evolving institution that reflects care, creativity, and deep community
  30| investment.
  31| We continue to make large and small changes to the library in an effort to constantly improve the facility, our
  32| resources, and the value the library brings to the community.
  33| This year we made significant strides in improving the comfort and sustainability of our building. The
  34| installation of mini splits, along with essential HVAC repairs, has greatly enhanced efficiency and

===PAGE 56=== (plain, 42 lines)
   1| responsiveness throughout the library. Although the HVAC is aging and maintenance needs continue to arise,
   2| we saw a drastic improvement in the system’s efficiency after a repair in August.
   3| The exterior of the library received much-needed attention, including painting and general maintenance made
   4| possible by American Rescue Plan act funding. This work not only preserves the integrity of the building but
   5| also reinforces the library’s presence as a well-cared-for and inviting landmark in our town. Similarly, the new
   6| library sign that was added at the end of FY24 to the façade received lighting fixtures as its final touch.
   7| Gardens, Grounds, and Stewardship
   8| The Proctor Memorial Garden once again has a fully functioning waterfall. Another project that was completed
   9| thanks to ARPA funding, this work restores the patio and its surrounds to a condition that fully supports
  10| mindful appreciation of our environment, quiet contemplation, and even energetic play for young library
  11| visitors.
  12| We are grateful to Charles LeTarte for the generous donation of two handcrafted bird houses. These charming
  13| additions enhance the garden spaces in the front of the library and reflect the library’s commitment to local
  14| wildlife and environmental awareness.
  15| We also embraced a “Leave Your Leaves” approach in designated garden areas to support luna moth habitats.
  16| Our three River Birch trees on the southeastern corner of the building could support luna moths over the winter
  17| if the leaves are allowed to remain on the ground around the trees. This simple but meaningful practice
  18| reinforces our objectives to educate and demonstrate acts that support our local ecosystems.
  19| Programs, Outreach, and Community Engagement
  20| We kicked off our year with our best ever Summer Reading Program. Almost 400 people registered their
  21| reading endeavors, while hundreds of others attended the programming events. The highlight even more than
  22| the high levels of participation this year was our summer lunch program, sponsored by Main Street Bank,
  23| during which we served almost 650 lunches to Summer Reading Program participants and other visitors to the
  24| library. Both the library and Main Street Bank are excited to continue this partnership during future Summer
  25| Reading Programs.
  26| During FY25, we also developed our focused outreach plan to guide our efforts to connect with underserved
  27| patrons and non-library users outside the library walls. Through visits to Farmers’ or Artisan Markets, schools,
  28| local businesses and apartment complexes, our goal is to find new avenues to deliver services to our
  29| community. I thoroughly believe that the library has something that could benefit each and EVERYONE in
  30| town, when they are aware of its availability.
  31| Spaces for Growth and Belonging
  32| If there is one accomplishment of the library this year to focus on, it’s the renovation of the Teen Room, which
  33| transformed the space into a vibrant, welcoming space designed with our teens in mind. The updated room
  34| supports study, creativity, and social connection, and clearly signals that young adults have a valued place in the
  35| library. Most importantly, it creates a safe, comfortable environment for teens to use library resources without
  36| unintentionally disrupting access for other groups. These changes were funded by ARPA money, and the
  37| furniture was purchased by our Friends of the Lunenburg Public Library. The Friends also offered additional
  38| funding to support contingency expenses for the construction project. Our Friends of the Lunenburg Public
  39| Library are unique for a library of our size in their capacity to provide continued advocacy and financial
  40| support, and they make it possible for us to respond thoughtfully to both planned improvements and unexpected
  41| needs.

  23|       The Lunenburg Public Access Cable Committee (PACC) is responsible for the long-term plan to manage the
  24|       Public Access Channels available to the Lunenburg community through Comcast, the town’s only cable-
  25|       service provider.
  26|       The overall strategy includes providing and improving equipment to acquire, record, broadcast and re-
  27|       broadcast programming.  Original content is also conceived and produced by PAC.  Town events/meetings
  28|       and school activities, as well as outside sources of programming, are all provided to increase the viewer’s
  29|       knowledge of what is happening around town.

===PAGE 61=== (plain, 37 lines)
   1| Two members of PACC resigned during FY25; Paul Sarapas and Pete Lincoln, leaving two vacancies on the
   2| committee.  Brian Vienneau joined the committee as the fourth member at the end of FY25.  There is one
   3| vacancy remaining.
   4| Programming
   5| CH8 – Government
   6| Most content on the Government Channel (Ch8) is locally broadcasted meetings.  In addition to several live
   7| weekly municipal meetings and re-broadcasts, other government programs downloaded from MassAccess
   8| MMX (massaccess.telvue.com), include Massachusetts State Agency PSA’s and programs of a political
   9| nature.
  10| There was an increase in local government meetings being recorded and uploaded to the government and
  11| YouTube channels, including the newly formed Trust Funds Committee, School Committee’s Superintendent
  12| Interview special meetings, Council on Aging, Stormwater Task Force, Economic Development Committee
  13| and special forums with the Master Plan Steering Committee.
  14| PAC produced “Talk of the Town” program in FY25, which is an interview program featuring the Town
  15| Manager.  This show airs on both the Government channel (Channel 8) and the Public Channel (Channel9).
  16| “Talk of the Town” is in the process of being revamped for FY26.
  17| Government meetings are recorded at the request of board/committee members and reviewed by PAC.  PAC
  18| makes every effort to accommodate requests based on availability.  Meetings are recorded and scheduled to
  19| rebroadcast on Ch8 and uploaded to the PAC’s YouTube Channel.  These YouTube meetings can be watched
  20| and/or downloaded at the convenience of viewers.  The number of rebroadcast meetings on Ch8 is over 150
  21| hours per month.  Rebroadcast meeting hours fluctuate depending on the time of year and number of meetings.
  22| CH9 – Public
  23| Public Access Cable (PAC) produced 75% of the local programming on Ch9 in FY25, down 3% from FY24.
  24| The total number of Public (Ch9) programs, both local and AccessShare (outside resources), decreased from
  25| 125 in FY24 to 80 programs in FY25 resulting in a decrease of overall programs of 36 %.  This decrease in
  26| Ch9 programs was due to the growth of government recordings, a reduction of videographers and the transfer
  27| of LHS sports from Public Channel (Ch9) to the Educational Channel (Ch22).
  28| Sixty (75%) local programs included presentations, band concerts and featured projects. The remaining 20
  29| (25%) programs were obtained through shared media sources.
  30| Several categories of local programming were aired on Public Ch9. Among the top programs were
  31| Informational (31%), Events (25%), and Entertainment (32%), making up the majority of Ch9 programming
  32| (see chart below).

  12| CH22 – Educational
  13| In May of FY20, PAC added an Educational Channel, Comcast Channel 22.  The additional channel has
  14| allowed PAC to feature local educational content to viewers in addition to the bi-monthly School Committee
  15| meetings.
  16| Many programs are shared between Channel 9 (Public) and Channel 22.  As of FY25, most of the channel’s
  17| content remains to be LHS sports, school events and concerts, as well as, downloaded resources such as
  18| “Democracy NOW” and “Kim’s Art Show.”  Other shows added to the channel have an educational or
  19| entertainment component to them, including “Wicked Good Food” and “Health Matters.”
  20| While it is optimal to receive programming from the local schools, PAC frequently subsidizes local
  21| programming with imported resources.  School Committee meetings, shared between Gov’t. (Ch8) and
  22| Educational (Ch22), airs frequently for the viewers convenience.  Other school events are recorded, often with
  23| the use of multiple cameras, as they occur throughout the year.
  24| “Lunenburg Storytime – The Books We Love” produced by PAC airs twice daily on Ch22 as an anchor of this
  25| channel.  Storytime has experienced tremendous popularity amongst residents as well as other media centers
  26| on the MMX database.  Community volunteers read children’s books in studio recorded monthly for
  27| broadcast.
  28| PAC continues to work toward content growth on all channels.

   9| into the schedule by helping to fulfill our commitment to the community.

  11| stations that air on Ch9, including “Barbara and You” and Chess Chat from Fitchburg Access Television

  13| Studio and Equipment
  14| PAC has had studio space in the TC Passios school since 2013.  We encourage the public to take advantage of
  15| the facilities and equipment offered for creative productions. The PAC manager also supports various town
  16| departments in the use of public access’ resources for their communication needs.
  17| In FY25 PAC completed the upgrade of the audio system in the Bilotta Room at Town Hall with a Symetrix
  18| system.  This improvement was paid for through ARPA funding.  The speaker system was replaced and the
  19| control room upgraded with a tablet-based control panel for audio administration.
  20| The audio quality now experienced at meetings has been remarkable and has exceeded expectations.
  21| The studio has continued to experience the benefits of the FY24 upgrades, including the new switcher and
  22| cameras.  In FY25, PAC has added more lighting kits, portable wireless microphones and new and reused
  23| furniture for the set.  Many organizations have taken advantage of the studio using it for purposes such as
  24| event announcements.
  25| Staff
  26| In FY25, there was one full-time Manager, a Production Technician, 5 part-time videographers and a part-time
  27| contracted Bulletin Administrator.  One videographer resigned, leaving 2 vacancies in the organization. One
  28| videographer was hired to fill the open position at the end of FY25, leaving one open videographer position
  29| for FY26.
  30| The PAC Manager administers the day-to-day operation of the organization, including all production and
  31| programming schedules, staff scheduling, equipment and services procurement, social media and equipment
  32| and system troubleshooting.  Videographers provide video recording of government meetings and are
  33| available for local video assignments and projects.
  34| The Production Technician manages the day-to-day operations of the studio and assists the videographers with
  35| training and equipment needs.  Reporting to the Manager, he provides technical assistance for production and
  36| studio support.  The team relies on the Production Technician to oversee and assist with troubleshooting issues
  37| that arise.  He also advises on new equipment and supervises set up and administration of large productions.
  38| PAC’s 5 Videographers work 2-10 hours per week recording board and committee meetings, sports, events
  39| and special projects.  They work “in the field” as well as in the studio producing such shows as “Talkin’
  40| Baseball” and “Movie Talk.”  The staff responds to recording requests from town officials and management on

===PAGE 64=== (layout, 39 lines)
   1| a regular basis and help cover larger productions such as the LHS home football games and Town Meetings,
   2| resulting in high quality 4 camera productions.
   3| Videographer coverage has been entered in Google Calendar since FY25, which streamlines the scheduling
   4| process.  A calendar link is sent to the staff at the end of the month listing their upcoming assignments and is
   5| available for all videographers to access.  Dates for coverage are assigned and automatic reminders are sent
   6| out 2 days before an event to the videographer’s email.
   7| PAC is always looking for producers.  If a community member has a special skill or interest, PAC will help
   8| make the show happen.  Our studio and staff are equipped to assist new producers in video production.

   9| Summary
  10| PAC experienced a significant decrease in Public Channel (Ch9) growth in FY25.  There were several
  11| reasons for the decline, including videographer’s hours and an increase in government meetings.  LHS
  12| sports were moved from Ch9 to the Educational Channel (Ch22) for the year, resulting in the decrease of
  13| public programming.  However, with careful planning and full videographer staff, PAC’s goal is to surpass
  14| FY25 growth in FY26.
  15| PAC offers more informational, entertainment and event category programs to the community.  These
  16| programs are popular on our stations, as well as on the Lunenburg Access YouTube channel.  Viewers are
  17| able to access a wide variety of shows, including concerts and LHS sports.  Content has been created with
  18| minimal staff, as videographers juggled multiple commitments to deliver local programming.
  19| While our shared PAC programming on MassAccess’ MMX database steadily grew in popularity, PAC’s
  20| local programming experienced a declined.  The MMX database content uploaded for sharing, include our
  21| popular featured PAC produced programs.  These shows are a strong representation of PAC’s ability to
  22| create quality content in the upgraded studio. The Educational Channel (Ch22) programming remains at a
  23| consistent rate of growth, while Government (Ch8) has increased with the addition of committee/board
  24| meetings.
  25| PAC staff is the core of the group.  The team is supportive and dedicated to the goals of the organization.
  26| Videographers are always learning new skills and training on new equipment.  They also continually cover
  27| hybrid board and committee meetings as requested without hesitation.  There are currently over 20 board
  28| and committee meetings that are recorded either through Zoom or in hybrid mode.  While often short
  29| staffed, PAC videographers have managed to keep up with government recordings and local shows of
  30| interest.
