  15|                             SENIOR PROPERTY TAX WORK-OFF PROGRAM
  16|                                           JANUARY 1, 2025 – NOVEMBER 1, 2025
  17| The Senior Property Tax Work-Off Committee is administered by the Assistant Town Manager/HR Director.
  18| What is the Senior Property Tax Work-Off?
  19| The Senior Property Tax Work-Off Program offers income eligible senior citizens age 60+ an opportunity to
  20| have an abatement applied to their property tax bill. Participants work in various town departments doing jobs
  21| such as general office work, custodial, library shelving, meals on wheels, school assistance, etc., to earn the tax
  22| abatement.
  23| The 2025 tax abatement maximum is $1,500 and applied to the participant’s 3rd quarter real estate tax bill.
  24| The current hourly rate is $15.00 per hour.
  25| Eligibility Requirements
  26| · Applicants must be 60 years of age or older
  27| · Must occupy and be the owner of the property as of July 1st
  28| · Receive a property tax bill in their name or their spouse’s name (60 years+)
  29| · Meet the income guidelines of (proof of income is required):
  30|      one person household - $50,000
  31|      two person household - $75,000
  32|  · All new applicants are required to have a CORI background check
  33|  · Earnings are exempt             from state taxes
  34| · Earnings are subject to OBRA if participants are not receiving a pension from either
  35| Worcester Regional Retirement or Massachusetts State Teachers Retirement
  36| · Final amount earned will be applied to the 3rd quarter real estate tax
  37| · All Property Tax Workers must re           -apply and be accepted annually for participation in the
  38|   program

  10|                                                  SEWER COMMISSION
  11| The Sewer Commission bears the responsibility of overseeing the Sewer Enterprise Fund, planning for the
  12| future, and developing and implementing rules, regulations, and policies. Under the Town’s Charter,
  13| responsibility for the day            -to-day operation, care and maintenance of the sanitary sewers are under the
  14| supervision of the Town Manager who delegates the responsibility to manage and maintain the operational side
  15| of the system to the Department of Public Works’ Director. The Town of Lunenburg does not operate a sewer
  16| treatment plant. Approximately 89% of Lunenburg sewer is discharged to the City of Leominster, and the other
  17| 11% is discharged to the City of Fitchburg.
  18| The Sewer Commission started FY25 with the following members: John Reynolds-Chair, Brett Ramsden-Vice
  19| Chair, and Mike Mackin as Clerk.  At the end of August, John Reynolds stepped down from the Commission,
  20| leaving only 2 members. A mailing was sent out to all sewer customers, seeking new members. Four men
  21| applied and three new commissioners started on 9/24/24. With a full board, the Commission reorganized with
  22| Mike Mackin (Chair), Brett Ramsden (Vice Chair), Scott Dall (Clerk) and members Joe Hurley and Eli Torres.
  23| In early 2025 Mike Mackin and Eli Torres left the Commission but were replaced in May by Dan Proctor and
  24| Arthur Katis.
  25| At the end of August 2024, Paula Bertram resigned as Sewer Business Manager and it was several months
  26| before a replacement was found.  In the meantime, DPW Director Bill Bernard stepped in as acting Business
  27| Manager, in addition to running the DPW, and Paula consulted part-time assisting Bill with quarterly billing
  28| plus other tasks.  Andrew Valliere was hired in January 2025 and quickly learned the job with some training
  29| from Paula.  During all this transition, there were still multiple issues with doing the billing on Munis.  Outside
  30| consultants were brought in to enable the bills to go out relatively on time.  To Andrew’s credit, he persevered
  31| through some tough billing cycles and found ways to deal with the Munis issues. In May 2025, Susan Sullivan
  32| was hired as Assistant Sewer Business Manager.
  33| Currently there are 1,226 properties connected to the Lunenburg system and another 270 which have access to
  34| Town Sewer but are not yet connected. During FY25, 14 new accounts connected to Town Sewer. The
  35| Commission billed out $1,187,341.09 in quarterly sewer bills and $67,187.77 went to owners’ December 2024
  36| FY25 tax bills for non-payment of sewer charges. The delinquency rate has been averaging 18% and continues
  37| to be an issue.
  38| The Commission received $100,000 in ARPA funds for repairs to manholes that are allowing clean water to
  39| enter the system as I/I (Inflow & Infiltration).  The Manhole Repair IFB went out in September 2024 and the
  40| contract was awarded to Insituform Technologies for replacement of frames and covers, along with repairs to
  41| the inside of some manholes.  Due to various delays, work was scheduled to begin in July 2025.
  42| Major repair projects were completed in FY25 at the Mass 1 and Dana Street pump stations by our maintenance

===PAGE 68=== (layout, 39 lines)
   1| contractor (CTE) and sub-contractor Pride Environmental.  The repair at Mass 1 involved replacing a rotting
   2| pipe under the station, repairing suction lines and replacing the gate valves at a cost of $98,000. The work was
   3| completed in November 2024. The Dana Street station is the main pump station that most of the waste goes
   4| through. It also had some rotting pipes that needed replacement similar to Mass 1 and the project was scheduled
   5| for the end of June 2025 at an estimated cost of $123,600.  As the pump stations are approaching 20 years of
   6| use, these projects will protect the stations from very costly emergency repairs.
   7| As in FY24, clogs in the pump stations continued to be a major concern. The Commission sent out reminders to
   8| users and placed notices in the Lunenburg Ledger noting how important it is to only flush waste and toilet paper
   9| down the system. Clogs jam the pumps and can cause costly repairs, which can impact sewer costs.
  10| At the 5/3/25 Annual Town Meeting, the Commission put forward 4 articles. The FY26 budget article
  11| appropriated $1,886,150.22 from anticipated Sewer Enterprise receipts of $1,583,917.45 and $302,232.77 from
  12| Retained Earnings to balance the budget. The second article transferred monies to the Capital Reserve
  13| Stabilization Fund in the amount of $5,133.15.The third warrant article transferred $19,104.40 into the Sewer
  14| Inflow/Infiltration Stabilization Fund used for mitigating I/I from entering the system. The fourth article
  15| transferred the sum of $1,545.00 into the OPEB Sewer Trust Fund. All four articles passed at Town Meeting.

  24|                                                         VETERANS’ SERVICES
  25| Massachusetts leads the way in taking care of Veterans because only in MA, is there a Veterans Service
  26| Officers in every Town, either Full Time (Population over 12,000) or Part Time.
  27| Also, MA is the only State that offers Chapter 115 Benefits to its Veterans, Veterans families, or widows who
  28| qualify, can be provided this monthly financial assistance, which are reimbursements for specific living
  29| expenses such as heating fuel, medical care, and pharmacy co-payments.
  30| This Veteran Agent is State Certified by the Department of Veterans Affairs, so this Veteran Agent is an
  31| authorized representative, to process and file VA claims for Veterans benefits.
  32| Some other examples of Veterans’ Service Office assistance services include:
  33| --A                               ssistance obtaining military service records
  34| --Housing assistance, including Veterans Shelters and Veterans Homes
  35| --Payments of “Welcome Home” bonuses for deployed Veterans
  36| --Assistance obtaining certain Massachusetts automobile and motorcycle license plates
  37| --Employment assistance
  38| --Property tax exemptions
  39| --Tax Exempt State An                               nuities for parents or spouses of those killed in Action or those who are 100% disabled.

   7| Community Health Nursing
   8| Nashoba’s Community Health Nursing program provides an essential public health service to its member
   9| communities guided by the American Nurses Association (ANA) Standards of Public Nursing Practice.  Our
  10| nursing team underwent significant changes this year, a retirement and staff moving to new positions.  As of the
  11| end of 2025 the nursing team has been rebuilt, and we are working quickly to restore services while remaining
  12| adaptable to changes requested by our member communities and to meet the obligations outlined in the FPHS.
  13| Town Nurse Hours were “on pause” July through December 2025 while we re-built our public health nursing
  14| team. During this time, the core, State            -mandated communicable disease case investigation and reporting
  15| continued.
  16| The Nashoba nursing team reviewed, investigated and reported on all mandated communicable and infectious
  17| diseases (including respiratory diseases) while working closely with the Massachusetts Department of Public
  18| Health’s (MDPH) epidemiology team. Though this daily reporting and investigation work is not always visible,
  19| it is vital to protect the public from the spread of disease and includes:
  20|          •                                                           Working with MDPH and local Boards of Health to identify and manage clusters of disease/exposures in
  21|                    the district.
  22|          •                                                           Working with school nurses and childcare providers in the district to provide information, offer advice
  23|                    and support.
  24|          •                                                           In conjunction with our Health Agents, we work with individuals in challenging living conditions
  25|                    (unsanitary, hoarded) to facilitate services to mitigate situations which would allow an individual to
  26|                    remain in their home.
  27|          •                                                           We work with Councils on Aging, community outreach workers and other staff in town to help residents
  28|                    find services they need.

  24|                                                               FIRE DEPARTMENT
  25|     The Firefighters and Emergency Medical Technicians of the Lunenburg Fire Department are dedicated to
  26| providing the highest quality, most cost-effective fire, and emergency medical services to the citizens of the town
  27|                                                                          of Lunenburg.
  28|            In 2025, your Fire Department responded to 2006 calls for service, which broke down as follows:
  29|                       Fires, Alarms & Hazardous Conditions                                       387
  30|                       Emergency Medical                                                        1233
  31|                       Inspections                                                                320
  32|                       Other                                                                        29
  33| This level of activity was similar to 2024, with a slight decrease in fires, alarms and hazardous conditions, but
  34| an increase in EMS responses.  The closure of Nashoba Valley Medical Center continues to strain the Region’s
  35| EMS Services.  Ambulances traveling to distant hospitals or “holding the wall” waiting for a bed locally have
  36| resulted in increased out of service times for all services in the area.  For our Department, this has resulted in a
  37| 36% increase in mutual aid EMS responses and an average of 15 additional minutes in turnaround time for an
  38| ambulance to become available.  It is not uncommon for one of the ambulances to be “holding the wall” in the
  39| local Emergency Department for 20 minutes or more waiting for a bed.
  40| The Department consists of 10 Career and 30-                                         35 On Call/Per Diem Firefighters and Emergency Medical
  41| Technicians, plus a full-time Administrative Assistant. The Station is staffed by three Firefighter/EMT’s or
  42| Paramedics. This coverage is provided by a combination of our Career Staff and Per Diem Firefighters. The

===PAGE 76=== (layout, 45 lines)
   1| greatest issue we continue to confront is having enough part time staff to cover the 96 hours of Per Diem
   2| coverage each week.  This is particularly true of having enough Part time Firefighter/Paramedics.  The addition
   3| of a 4th   shift of 3 Firefighter/Paramedics is critical to our future operations.  This would allow Career Staff to
   4| cover 7 days per week, not 6.  This would improve working conditions for our staff and decrease the amount of
   5| forced overtime we are experiencing.  The Per diem coverage could then be reallocated to assist with staffing
   6| our second ambulance for much of the week.  This is a concern that is coming to the forefront with increasing
   7| numbers of ambulance calls and longer transport and turnaround times at hospitals.  In 2025 we had to rely on
   8| mutual aid 65 times for a mutual aid ambulance.  This was due to either insufficient staffing to cover the second
   9| ambulance, an ambulance being out of service or both ambulances were already on calls.
  10| Staffing the Station with dual trained Fire/EMS personnel ensures that we are prepared to respond to whatever
  11| emergency occurs. As many calls require more personnel than are on duty, we continue to rely heavily on the
  12| dedication and commitment of our On Call Firefighters and Emergency Medical Technicians.
  13| The Department’s Paramedic Program is now in its third year.  Having this level of service in-                   house allows us
  14| to provide advanced level EMS care to our residents and not draw on resources from other communities.  Of the
  15| Staff on Duty, One-two are always Firefighter/Paramedics. Paramedic training is more than two thousand hours
  16| and requires anywhere from 9-                       18 months of college level classroom education, clinical time, and field
  17| internships to obtain certification. Firefighter/Paramedics Andrew Bolton and Jenny Smith serve as our ALS
  18| and EMS Coordinators.
  19| Lieutenant Christos Lekaditis and Firefighter Carl Gamberdella make up the Department’s Fire Prevention
  20| Division and conducted 350 Inspections in 2025. This is in addition to multiple fire drills and public education
  21| initiatives. By law, we are required to inspect Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detector installations when a home
  22| is sold. We are also required to inspect all new oil burners and propane gas installations. Any business holding a
  23| liquor license also requires a yearly inspection for fire safety issues. In addition, all new construction projects
  24| must have their plans reviewed for proper fire protection, as well as ongoing inspections during the construction
  25| process. Other Fire Safety Initiatives undertaken during 2025 include:
  26|     -                                    Continuation of a Department of Fire Services Grant in the amount of $6953 to assist with Fire Safety
  27|          Education in both the schools and with Senior Citizens. This Grant provides funding for both materials
  28|          and personnel to bring fire safety education to our most vulnerable populations. Firefighter Olivia Hayes
  29|          serves as our Coordinator for this program.
  30|     -                           Participation in the Senior Center’s “Sand for Seniors” Program. This program provides buckets of
  31|          walkway sand for Senior Citizens who were unable to obtain it for themselves in the winter months. In
  32|          partnership with this program, Firefighter Olivia Hayes delivers the sand to the residents and when
  33|          possible, inspects their homes for Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors. If the resident was lacking
  34|          detectors, Firefighter Hayes can install free detectors obtained through the Senior SAFE Grant.
  35|     -                             It should be noted that each year, 50% of fatal fires are found to have nonfunctional or nonexistent
  36|          smoke detectors.
  37| Fire Prevention has become increasingly complex as codes change and new technologies appear. To keep pace,
  38| both Inspectors hold certifications with the State as Fire Prevention Officers-     Level 1 or 2.  In addition two
  39| other members have also completed the Level one training and other staff have completed the Basic Level
  40| training.
  41| Four Firefighters from Lunenburg continue to be members of the Fire District 8 Technical Rescue and Dive
  42| Teams. These regional teams respond to high risk and specialized rescue situations, such as Confined Space,
  43| Rescue from Heights, Building and Trench Collapse, Swift/Floodwater and Underwater Search and Recovery.
  44| In conjunction with these Teams, Lunenburg operates both a Water Rescue Unit and a Collapse/Trench Rescue
  45| Trailer.

===PAGE 77=== (layout, 37 lines)
   1| Our Apparatus fleet is currently in particularly good condition, with two pumpers and the Ladder truck at or
   2| under 10 years old. Engine 2, our 1989 GMS Brush Fire Truck, has exceeded its lifespan and is currently
   3| scheduled for replacement under the proposed FY ’27 Capital Plan.  Our Rescue Pumper, Squad 3, remains in
   4| good condition though it is nearing the end of its projected life span. This unit is scheduled for Replacement in
   5| FY’29. This unit is a dual-purpose Pumper and Rescue Unit, carrying the Jaws of Life, High Pressure Air Bags,
   6| and other specialized rescue tools.
   7| The Ambulances are experiencing increased wear and tear as we see not only more calls for service but longer
   8| transport times to more distant hospitals and critical care facilities. 35 years ago, we had four hospitals within a
   9| 10–15-minute transport time. Today there is only one. In addition, many cardiac and trauma patients require
  10| definitive treatment in specialty facilities. This often requires transport to Worcester or occasionally even
  11| Boston.   Our new Rescue 1 arrived in the spring of 2025 and is in service as our Primary Ambulance.  Rescue
  12| 2, a 2019 unit has been rotated to be the back up ambulance.  The former Rescue 1, a 2014 International has
  13| been rotated to replace our water rescue truck which was a 1998 ambulance.
  14| State and Federal Grants provided additional equipment to the Department including:
  15|     -                                              Drying Rack for drying firefighting clothing after washing/decontamination
  16|     -                                              Replaced broken/obsolete chain saws
  17|     -                                              New Forest Fire Helmets and gloves to replace ones over 20 years old
  18|     -                                              2 Handheld Thermal Imaging Cameras
  19| As I write what will be my last Town Report before my retirement, I must reflect on the progress the Fire
  20| Department has made in the last 13 years.  When I assumed the role of Fire Chief in 2012, much of our front-
  21| line apparatus was approaching or over 20 years old.  Our staffing only provided 2-                                             3 Firefighters during the
  22| day.  Our On Call staff responded to all calls after 6pm.   We relied on other services to provide Advanced Life
  23| Support for our ambulance patients.  Today nearly all our front-line apparatus has been updated and is 10 years
  24| or less in age.  We have 24/7 coverage at the Station and provide our own Advanced Life Support.  These
  25| improvements were possible due to the unwavering support of Town residents, Town Government and most of
  26| all the men and women of the Lunenburg Fire Department.  It is my fervent wish that this support continues to
  27| bring the Department over its next great hurdle.  The need for the 4th Shift.
  28| In conclusion, I would like to thank the members of the Lunenburg Fire Department for their outstanding
  29| commitment to the Town. Their enthusiasm, professionalism and dedication are what truly make the
  30| Department the high-                                 quality organization that it is.  I do not say it enough, but so many of our staff deserve
  31| accolades for the work they do “behind the scenes” every day to make the Department what it is. I cannot ask
  32| for a better group of men and women, and it is my profound honor to have served with them.
  33| I would also like to thank the other department heads, boards, and commissions for their continuing support
  34| during my tenure The level of inter-departmental cooperation that occurs daily is invisible to most people, but it
  35| continues to be critical to the smooth operation of the Town. Finally, my thanks also go out to the citizens of
  36| Lunenburg for their ongoing support of public safety. Such support allows us to continue providing the high
  37| level of service you have come to expect from us.

   2| Mission Statement:
   3| We, the members of the Lunenburg Police Department, strive to provide the highest quality of police services to
   4| our community members and visitors alike.  We believe in Community Policing, and all the benefits that are
   5| realized from this concept.  We will strive to maintain the strong partnerships that have been developed with our
   6| community and continuously look for ways to improve that relationship.  We will strive to deliver police
   7| services in a fair and impartial manner, consistent with all applicable laws, while respecting all individual
   8| rights.  We will use innovative and modern ideas and techniques to solve crimes, apprehend criminal offenders,
   9| and help resolve quality of life issues.
  10| Values:
  11|      •                                           We are committed to ensuring that all of our actions reflect the utmost integrity and honesty.
  12|      •                                           We are committed to respecting individual rights, human dignity, and the values of all members of the
  13|           community and members of the Lunenburg Police Department.
  14|      •                                           We are a proactive and problem-solving agency.
  15|      •                                           We strive to serve our citizens in a professional manner with compassion, respect, and empathy.
  16|      •                                           We are committed to providing the highest quality of police services to our community.
  17|      •                                           We recognize the value of our employees and recognize they are our most valued resource.  We will
  18|           strive to provide our employees with the necessary resources, training, and career development to
  19|           enhance their professionalism.
  20|      •                                           We recognize that the well-being of our employees is of the utmost importance.  We will strive to
  21|           provide the necessary assistance to assure our employees enjoy a long and satisfying career.

   1| Department Review:
   2| It is a privilege to present the Lunenburg Police Department’s Annual Report. In 2025, the Department
   3| continued to face challenges related to economic conditions, population growth, increased traffic and increase
   4| of cyber-crimes involving within the community. Ongoing nationwide difficulties in police recruitment and
   5| retention have also impacted the Department; however, progress has been made in addressing these challenges.
   6| Despite these obstacles, the Department remains proactive and fully committed to ensuring the safety of the
   7| community.
   8| Promotions:
   9| In October 2024, Chief Thomas Gammel retired, and Lieutenant Jeffrey Thibodeau was promoted to Interim
  10| Chief of Police. In November 2024, Sergeant Sean Zrate was promoted to Acting Lieutenant. Both positions
  11| later became permanent. In 2025, Interim Chief Thibodeau was formally appointed Chief of Police in April, and
  12| Acting Lieutenant Zrate was appointed to the rank of Lieutenant in August.
  13| New-Hire Updates:
  14| In May 2025, Officer Brody Tapply was appointed as a student officer and attended the Basic Recruit Academy
  15| at Fitchburg State University. Upon successfully completing the academy, he was sworn in as a full-time patrol
  16| officer in September 2025.
  17| In October 2025, the Department welcomed two additional officers, Officer Grace Kerr and Officer Elijah
  18| Weiss. Officer Kerr is a graduate of Fitchburg State University and previously served with the Fitchburg State
  19| University Police Department beginning in September 2023. Officer Weiss joined the Department from the
  20| Mendon Police Department, where he served since October 2023. Prior to that, he was employed by Fitchburg
  21| State University from 2021 through 2023.
  22| Programming Updates:
  23| Through a partnership with the Lancaster Police Department and Open Sky Community Services, the
  24| Department was able to secure funding to implement a Co-Response Model for mental health–related calls. As
  25| a result, Co-Response Clinician Vanessa Rivera began working with the Department in December. This
  26| program enhances our ability to respond effectively to mental health incidents and support community members
  27| during mental health                                                            related calls, as they             continue to increase.             The department has addressed the emerging
  28| nationwide trend of cyber-crimes and fraud. We have been fortunate to have highly trained and proactive
  29| Officers with the expertise and guidance of Officer Bradley McNamara in combatting these cyber-crime trends.
  30| Officer McNamara has had many successful prosecutions and seizure of illicit funds that lead to the victims
  31| recovering their financial loses.
  32| 2025 Statistical Information:
  33| The overall goal of the Lunenburg Police Department is a reduction of crime, assure quality of life issues are
  34| addressed, and provide a safe community to live, work and visit.  The Department evaluates effectiveness, in
  35| part, by statistical information that is generated through the Records Management System.
  36| The following statistical information is to provide some insight into our officers’ activity for 2025.

   4| Nashoba Valley Regional Dispatch District:
   5| The Nashoba Valley Regional Dispatch District (NVRDD) is a Regional Emergency Communications Center
   6| located in Devens, MA. NVRDD serves as the 911 public safety answering point and dispatch center for Police,
   7| Fire and EMS for the communities of Lunenburg, Berlin, Bolton, Boxborough, Havard, Lancaster, Devens,
   8| Hudson and Department of Defense at Devens.  NVRDD serves a total population of just over 55,000 residents
   9| and thousands more visitors to the orchards, farms, businesses, and attractions within its eight communities.

   1|                                           LUNENBURG PUBLIC SCHOOLS
   2|                                                  Superintendent’s Message
   3| To the Citizens of Lunenburg,
   4| It is with profound joy and a deep sense of honor that I submit my first annual report as your Superintendent of
   5| Schools. As I conclude my first year in this role, I reflect on the warm welcome I have received from this
   6| community. I extend my deepest gratitude to the Town Manager, Town Department Heads, the Select Board,
   7| the Finance Committee, and the School Committee for their partnership and support. It is a privilege to serve a
   8| town that cares so deeply about its children.
   9| My tenure began with a commitment to listen. Before setting a new course, I needed to understand the heart of
  10| Lunenburg. Through three comprehensive surveys and countless conversations, I heard from 491 students, 106
  11| staff members, and 186 families.
  12| What I learned was powerful. I discovered a district with a strong heartbeat; where staff take immense pride in
  13| their colleagues and where families value the safety and opportunities our schools provide. However, I also
  14| heard clear calls for growth. While 70% of our students feel supported, we learned that a sense of belonging is
  15| fragile; too many students told us they do not yet feel fully accepted for who they are. Families expressed a
  16| need for stability in the budget and a focus on student mental health, while staff highlighted that years of fiscal
  17| constraints have impacted trust.
  18| These findings became the compass for our work this year. They confirmed that our mission must be to move
  19| our "One Community" spirit from a theme to a daily practice: welcoming all, lifting each other up, learning with
  20| purpose, and leading with heart.
  21| Guided by what I learned, we established four strategic goals to steer the district through the 2025- 2026 school
  22| year.
  23| First, we focused on Improving Instruction. With the appointment of Dr. Kimberly Sarfde as our Director of
  24| Teaching and Learning, we raised the bar for classroom excellence. Our goal has been to ensure every educator
  25| receives high-quality, actionable feedback that drives student achievement. A central pillar of this work is our
  26| steadfast commitment to early literacy, with the explicit goal that every child will be reading fluently by the end
  27| of third grade. We are seeing the "joy of rigor" emerge in every classroom, where high expectations meet high
  28| engagement.
  29| Second, we prioritized Fiscal Leadership and Transparency. A critical step in this direction was the hiring of
  30| Christopher McNamara as our Business Manager. Mr. McNamara has made strong gains in implementing
  31| accounting practices that are clear and publicly communicated, allowing effective insight for town elected
  32| officials and citizens. Understanding the financial pressures facing the town, we developed a budget process
  33| defined by "radical clarity." We presented distinct budget scenarios—level                                                -service, town-allocation, and
  34| restoration which fostered an honest, collaborative dialogue about what we value and what we fund.
  35| Third, we dedicated ourselves to Building a Culture of Belonging. We strove to create an environment where
  36| kindness is the norm and every student sees themselves as a valued member of the community.
  37| Looking back on the past year, we have achieved milestones.
  38| We completed universal screenings in mathematics and literacy for grades K            –5 to ensure no child slips through
  39| the cracks. Our educators modeled the instructional excellence we strive for. To support this work, we provided
  40| targeted professional development in the Open Sci Ed curriculum and the development of literacy skills.

===PAGE 89=== (layout, 41 lines)
   1| We built from a position of fiscal stability. Throughout the year, our budget remained healthy and on track. Our
   2| mantra was no surprises for the staff, school committee and the community that entrusts us to be stewards of
   3| limited resources.  Furthermore, in compliance with state requirements, we responsibly reinvested funds into
   4| our food services program, upgrading critical infrastructure like walk-in freezers to better serve our students.
   5|  The spirit of Lunenburg shone brightly this year. From the always spirited Homecoming parade to an
   6| undefeated regular season for our Field Hockey team and a Championship title for our Football team, our
   7| students gave us much to cheer for. Perhaps most inspiring was our Unified Basketball program, which
   8| continues to be a beacon of inclusion, proving that we win when we play together. Even in our youngest grades,
   9| we saw this culture taking root, with Primary School students demonstrating unprompted acts of kindness that
  10| remind us all of the power of empathy.
  11| As we look toward the coming year, my commitment to the town of Lunenburg remains steadfast: to lead
  12| visibly, communicate plainly, and budget transparently. We acknowledge the challenges ahead, but we face
  13| them with the strength of a united community.
  14| Thank you for the opportunity to serve this incredible town.
  15| Respectfully submitted,
  16| Dr. Jodi Fortuna, Superintendent

  37|                                                      Teaching & Learning Update
  38|                                                             Town Report 2025
  39| Teaching and learning remains the central focus of Lunenburg Public Schools. During the 2024–2025 school
  40| year, the district continued to strengthen curriculum implementation, instructional practices, and systems of
  41| student support across all grade levels. This work reflects a sustained commitment to research-based instruction,
  42| data-informed decision-making, and long-term instructional coherence, carried out amid ongoing fiscal
  43| constraints and increasing uncertainty in state and federal funding.
  44| Collectively, these instructional systems are designed to ensure that students receive consistent, high-quality

===PAGE 95=== (layout, 43 lines)
   1| instruction every day, regardless of school or grade level. The district’s emphasis on strong core instruction,
   2| early identification of need, and timely, targeted support is intended to prevent small gaps from becoming long-
   3| term barriers to learning. For students and families, this work results in clearer expectations, earlier
   4| intervention, and improved access to grade-level learning.
   5| Across content areas, the district has prioritized instructional approaches that emphasize conceptual
   6| understanding, reasoning, and application while maintaining alignment with the Massachusetts Curriculum
   7| Frameworks and expectations established by the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary
   8| Education.
   9| Literacy Instruction and Student Support Systems
  10| Lunenburg Public Schools continues to implement a coherent, research-aligned literacy system designed to
  11| improve outcomes for all students while maximizing the impact of limited and increasingly uncertain resources.
  12| Rather than relying on isolated or short-term initiatives, the district has focused on aligning curriculum,
  13| assessment, professional learning, and intervention into an integrated system that can be sustained over time.
  14| High-quality Tier 1 classroom instruction serves as the foundation of the district’s literacy framework. Research
  15| consistently demonstrates that strong daily instruction is the most effective way to improve literacy outcomes at
  16| scale, particularly in districts with limited supplemental staffing. At the elementary level (Grades K–5), HMH
  17| Into Reading provides a structured, evidence-based approach that integrates foundational skills, vocabulary
  18| development, knowledge-building, and comprehension.
  19| In Grades K–2, instruction emphasizes early reading development—including phonological awareness, phonics,
  20| spelling, and fluency—while intentionally embedding oral language and comprehension from the outset. These
  21| practices are designed to prevent reading difficulty rather than respond after gaps widen. In Grades 3–5,
  22| instruction shifts toward consolidating fluent reading and strengthening vocabulary, background knowledge,
  23| and comprehension of increasingly complex texts.
  24| At the middle school level, the district has devoted significant time to deepening implementation of Amplify
  25| English Language Arts. Educators engage in sustained Professional Learning Community (PLC) work focused
  26| on text complexity, pacing, instructional routines, and scaffolding to ensure students consistently engage with
  27| rigorous, grade-level material while receiving appropriate instructional support.
  28| Assessment data are used instructionally to guide teaching and support decisions. Elementary students are
  29| universally screened using Dynamic Indicators of Basic Literacy Skills (DIBELS)                                   , enabling educators to
  30| identify risk early, adjust instruction, and provide targeted intervention through the district’s Multi-Tiered
  31| System of Supports (MTSS). Intervention time and intensity are determined by data and refined through regular
  32| progress monitoring and collaborative review.
  33| Beginning in February 2026, Lunenburg Primary School will engage in a short, high-impact partnership with
  34| the HILL for Literacy. This classroom-based work will focus on modeling effective instruction and providing
  35| real-time feedback to teachers, intentionally strengthening internal instructional capacity that can be sustained
  36| despite declining external funding.
  37| Mathematics Instruction and Conceptual Understanding
  38| Mathematics instruction across grades K–12 emphasizes conceptual understanding, reasoning, and application
  39| rather than rote memorization of procedures. Programs and practices are aligned with the Massachusetts
  40| Mathematics Frameworks and DESE expectations for high-quality instruction.
  41| In Grades K–5, mathematics instruction is delivered through HMH Into Math                                                                                                            , with a strong emphasis on
  42| number sense, multiple representations, mathematical discourse, and problem-solving. Students regularly
  43| engage with visual models, hands-on materials, and structured discussion to develop deep and lasting

===PAGE 96=== (layout, 40 lines)
   1| understanding of mathematical concepts.
   2| At the middle school level, mathematics instruction is delivered through EdGems                                                                                                            , an inquiry-based program
   3| that emphasizes reasoning, sense-making, and productive struggle. Instruction encourages students to articulate
   4| their thinking, engage with complex problems, and develop confidence as mathematical learners.
   5| At the high school level, mathematics instruction follows a coherent sequence aligned with state frameworks
   6| and college- and career-readiness expectations. Students complete required coursework in Algebra, Geometry,
   7| and Algebra II, with additional opportunities in Precalculus, Statistics, Calculus, Business Math, and Advanced
   8| Placement courses. Multiple pathways ensure access to rigorous, standards-aligned instruction that supports a
   9| range of postsecondary goals.
  10| Universal screening for early numeracy using the Universal Screener for Number Sense (USNS) supports
  11| MTSS decision-making in the elementary grades. Data are reviewed collaboratively to guide instruction,
  12| intervention, and progress monitoring.
  13| Science Instruction and Inquiry-Based Learning
  14| Science instruction across grades K–12 is aligned with the Massachusetts Science and Technology/Engineering
  15| Frameworks and the Next Generation Science Standards. Instruction emphasizes inquiry, investigation, and the
  16| application of scientific concepts.
  17| In Grades K–2, science instruction is delivered through locally designed, standards-aligned units that promote
  18| curiosity, observation, questioning, and hands-on exploration, supporting early scientific thinking and language
  19| development.
  20| In Grades 3–5, science instruction utilizes OpenSciEd                                     materials, which engage students in real            -world
  21| phenomena and integrate science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and crosscutting concepts.
  22| This approach supports sustained investigation, explanation, and sense-making over time.
  23| Middle school science is delivered through Glencoe/McGraw Hill iScience, incorporating hands-on
  24| investigations, laboratory experiences, literacy connections, and assessments aligned with state standards.
  25| At the high school level, students complete coursework in Biology and have additional opportunities in
  26| Chemistry, Physics, Environmental Science, Anatomy and Physiology, Biotechnology, and Advanced
  27| Placement sciences. Instruction emphasizes laboratory experiences, scientific inquiry, and the application of
  28| scientific concepts.
  29| Data-Informed Instruction, MTSS, and Professional Collaboration
  30| Across content areas, structured data review and professional collaboration remain central to instructional
  31| improvement. Professional Learning Communities meet regularly to analyze student performance, refine
  32| instructional practices, and adjust MTSS supports. Progress is reviewed through ongoing data analysis,
  33| classroom observation, and collaborative reflection to ensure instructional practices remain effective, equitable,
  34| and responsive to student need.
  35| This work reflects the expertise, professionalism, and sustained commitment of Lunenburg educators, who
  36| continue to refine practice and support students despite significant resource constraints.
  37| Safety, Preparedness, and School Environment
  38| Student and staff safety remains a district priority. Staff have participated in ALICE safety training, and schools
  39| maintain strong partnerships with local police and fire departments to support emergency preparedness and age-
  40| appropriate safety education.

===PAGE 97=== (layout, 40 lines)
   1| Federal and State Funding: Strategic Use and Uncertainty
   2| The district continues to use federal ESSA Title funds strategically to support instructional priorities,
   3| professional learning, intervention services, and capacity-building aligned with identified student needs.
   4| However, the future of these funding sources is increasingly uncertain.
   5| Lunenburg Public Schools does not anticipate receiving its full allocation of Title I            funds in future years and is
   6| actively planning for potential reductions. In addition, the district is preparing for the likely loss of Title II            and
   7| Title IV funding moving forward. These funds have historically supported professional development,
   8| instructional leadership, and student support initiatives that cannot be readily absorbed into the local operating
   9| budget.
  10| As funding uncertainty increases, the district has prioritized protecting the instructional core. This includes
  11| maintaining high-quality curriculum, preserving early literacy and numeracy screening, sustaining MTSS
  12| structures, and ensuring educators have access to the professional collaboration necessary to respond effectively
  13| to student needs.
  14| The district is also actively pursuing additional grant opportunities to offset anticipated losses and support
  15| continued instructional improvement. Despite these efforts, the loss of federal funding will further limit
  16| flexibility and place additional pressure on already constrained instructional systems.
  17| Fiscal Context and Sustainability
  18| All instructional work described in this report has been carried out amid repeated budget reductions, staffing
  19| losses, declining grant funding, and growing uncertainty surrounding federal education dollars. These fiscal
  20| realities have required careful prioritization and an ongoing focus on instructional coherence and sustainability.
  21| The district is operating with limited remaining flexibility. Continued progress depends on stability in staffing
  22| and funding. Additional reductions—particularly the loss of federal Title funds—would compromise
  23| instructional systems and place current gains at risk.
  24| Looking Ahead
  25| Lunenburg Public Schools remains committed to continuous improvement, transparency, and collaboration with
  26| families and the community. The district’s instructional systems are designed to ensure that access to high
  27| quality instruction and timely support is based on student need rather than circumstance.
  28| By investing in coherent curriculum, strong instruction, and data-informed systems of support, the district
  29| continues to work toward improved outcomes for all students while responsibly managing limited and uncertain
  30| resources.
  31| Respectfully Submitted,
  32| Dr. Kimberly Sarfde, Director of Teaching & Learning

  30| Lunenburg Primary School
  31| Town Report 2025
  32| Lunenburg Primary School is a student-centered early childhood school serving children from preschool
  33| through Grade 2. Educating students ages three through eight, we remain committed to fostering a nurturing,
  34| inclusive, and engaging environment where each child’s academic, social, and emotional development is
  35| supported. Our school community consists of students, families, educators, instructional assistants, and support
  36| staff working collaboratively to ensure that every child’s individual needs are met. By focusing on the whole
  37| child, we strive to cultivate strong foundational academic skills alongside the essential social-emotional
  38| competencies that prepare students for continued success throughout their educational journey. We are proud to
  39| maintain a welcoming and enriching atmosphere where all children feel valued and encouraged to reach their
  40| full potential, and we look forward to another year of shared growth, learning, and community.
  41| As of February 2026, Lunenburg Primary School reported a total enrollment of 406 students to the Department
  42| of Elementary and Secondary Education. This includes 65 preschool students attending various half-day
  43| 94

===PAGE 99=== (plain, 48 lines)
   1| sessions across two classrooms. The school serves 110 Kindergarten students across five classrooms, with class
   2| sizes ranging from 21 to 23 students; 119 Grade 1 students across five classrooms, with class sizes of 23 to 24
   3| students; and 112 Grade 2 students across five classrooms, with class sizes ranging from 22 to 24 students. This
   4| structure ensures that each grade level is supported by dedicated classroom spaces designed to promote optimal
   5| learning conditions. We remain proud to provide a strong academic foundation that supports both student
   6| achievement and developmental growth.
   7| Throughout the 2025–2026 school year, our professional development efforts have centered on strengthening
   8| inclusive practices and refining high-quality instructional strategies. We continue to implement the HMH Into
   9| Reading and Into Math curricula to guide literacy and mathematics instruction. Common Planning Time
  10| remains a priority within our schedule, enabling teachers to collaborate regularly, analyze student performance
  11| data, and align instruction to meet the needs of all learners. In partnership with consultants and district
  12| curriculum coordinators, our staff continues to deepen the use of evidence-based practices and ensure a
  13| consistent and cohesive learning experience across grade levels.
  14| In addition to academic excellence, we place strong emphasis on cultivating a positive, inclusive, and
  15| supportive school culture. Our educators consistently work to create classroom environments where students
  16| feel safe, respected, and empowered. The Responsive Classroom model continues to be implemented school
  17| wide to strengthen community and promote social-emotional learning. We also maintain our commitment to
  18| Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS), a tiered framework designed to enhance student
  19| behavior and engagement through aligned systems and practices. Monthly school wide themes encourage
  20| reflection and character development among students and staff. Through our continued partnership with our
  21| School Resource Officer and his emotional support canine, Hank, we celebrate students through the Hank’s
  22| Helper Awards, recognizing acts of kindness, respect, and helpfulness within our school community. During
  23| monthly assemblies, selected students also participate in “Snack with the Principal,” providing opportunities for
  24| small-group connection and student voice. These initiatives reflect our dedication to supporting both academic
  25| achievement and character development.
  26| Lunenburg Primary School remains committed to ensuring that all students receive the support necessary to
  27| succeed. We continue refining our tiered instructional system to provide timely and targeted interventions.
  28| Students in Kindergarten through Grade 2 participate in common reading and mathematics assessments in the
  29| fall, winter, and spring to monitor progress and evaluate instructional effectiveness. Using this data, we identify
  30| students who may require additional support and provide targeted interventions through our Multi-Tiered
  31| System of Supports (MTSS). This year, we were pleased to secure two no-cost reading intervention programs
  32| for the district:  High Dosage Tutoring and Hill for Literacy to further strengthen our literacy support services.
  33| Our MTSS framework provides individualized interventions in reading, mathematics, speech and language,
  34| occupational therapy, and social-emotional support. Through a comprehensive and data-driven approach, we
  35| aim to ensure that every student is equipped with the tools and resources needed to thrive.
  36| The Lunenburg Primary School Council continues to meet monthly to review school initiatives, advise the
  37| principal, and contribute to the development of the school improvement plan and building budget. The 2025–
  38| 2026 Council members include Principal Carla Squier; Assistant Principal Michael Smith; parents Skylar Joly-
  39| Pelliter, Janet Winer, Sarah Wright, and Ryan Hilgendorf; School Committee Representative Mandy Gilman;
  40| and School Building Leadership Team members Jennifer Hochard, Amy Raffaele, Christa Palma, Julie Hudson,
  41| and Laura Refrigeri. The Council’s collaborative efforts and diverse perspectives ensure that decisions are made
  42| in the best interest of our students and school community.
  43| We are sincerely grateful for the opportunity to work alongside our dedicated district colleagues, supportive
  44| families, and engaged community partners in serving Lunenburg’s youngest learners. The continued
  45| collaboration and commitment of our school community make a meaningful difference in the lives of our
  46| students each day. For more information about Lunenburg Primary School, please visit the Lunenburg Primary
  47| School website.

  10|                                                    Turkey Hill Elementary School
  11|                                                             Town Report 2025
  12| Turkey Hill Elementary School is an elementary school serving students in third grade through fifth grade.  As
  13| of Feb 2026, Turkey Hill Elementary School serves                                                                                                                                                             355 enrolled students. There are five sections of grade 3,
  14| grade 4, and grade 5.  Grade 3 has 111 students. Grade 4 has 136 students and Grade 5 has 108 students.
  15| Our unified arts areas include physical education, art, music, library, and STEM. We are also served by a full
  16| time assistant principal, full time nurse, a psychologist, a full time adjustment counselor/social worker, and 21
  17| full time teachers.  Other support personnel who work across the district include an ELA coach (through
  18| December), a Math Specialist, a Director of Teaching and Learning, two EL teachers, a Speech and Language
  19| Pathologist, OT, and PT.  In addition, we have a half-time interventionist targeted support for small groups of
  20| students.
  21| Staff continually work on the development of the whole child by supporting students' development and growth
  22| in the areas of social emotional learning, literacy, math, social studies and science.  We are able to meet student
  23| needs with the support of the district curriculum of teaching and learning and the two coaches which enables
  24| teachers to have the opportunity to meet at grade levels to develop and provide evidence based instruction,
  25| common learning experiences, and student data analysis and share effective teaching strategies to support
  26| student academic growth.  Students continue to have benchmark assessments three times throughout the school
  27| year (beginning, middle and end of year) that are used to help us celebrate students’ academic growth and
  28| effort.   The data provided by these assessments also helps refine our focus for interventions.  We began the
  29| implementation of the OpenSci Ed curriculum with initial training and a trial unit.  The implementation will
  30| continue next school year.
  31| This fall our fifth grade students had their annual trip to Nature's Classroom. It was a successful week with good
  32| weather, community building, and the creation of fond memories of a unique time together, thanks to the
  33| combined efforts of our entire fifth grade staff.
  34| We held an open house in September. It was a well-attended event and for many parents their first opportunity
  35| to be physically present in our building.  It was accompanied by a book fair facilitated by our librarian, Mrs.
  36| McNamara. Parent conferences in January offered both in person and virtual options and appointments were
  37| fully booked within a few days.
  38| We held our annual Penny Wars fundraiser, it was a huge success and the money raised will be put toward the
  39| purchase and installation of a shade structure in our playing field.  As always, our PTO assisted in the weeklong
  40| collection. We could not be successful without their efforts. We were able to bring back a fifth grade band and
  41| all students will be performing in an upcoming spring concert under the direction of our music teacher, Mr.
  42| Anthony Balester.  Turkey Hill also held its annual Turkey Trot in November.  Led by Mr. Derek Guimond, the
  43| Turkey Trot was a wonderful experience.

  20|                                                         Lunenburg Middle School
  21|                                                              Town Report 2025
  22| Lunenburg Middle School provides a rigorous academic curriculum as well as strong programs that support
  23| students’ social and emotional growth. These programs ensure that each child becomes a self-motivated,
  24| creative, lifelong learner in a safe, stimulating environment that encourages diversity and open honest
  25| communication. The dedicated and accomplished staff of professionals within the school embraces the
  26| philosophy of educating the whole child academically, socially, and emotionally. This philosophy is a means by
  27| which all students become positive community members that possess the skills to be successful in high school
  28| and beyond.
  29|  Lunenburg Middle School is a co-located middle - high school serving grades six through eight. Our effective,
  30| student centered middle school embraces interdisciplinary teams of teachers that enable teachers to work with
  31| smaller groups of students. Smaller groups of students allow teachers to learn and engage students in their
  32| preferred learning style, making them more confident and successful.
  33| Our effective middle school model is student centered and provides opportunities to explore a variety of
  34| different interests and talents through special areas and enrichment classes and extracurricular activities. One of
  35| our goals is for students to discover something they are passionate about and want to continue exploring as they
  36| move through high school and beyond. We will continue to seek out opportunities for students that foster
  37| critical thinking and problem-solving skills that prepare them for high school and beyond or where their passion
  38| may lead them to.
  39| Our grade eight team of teachers continue to implement a schedule that mirrors the high school schedule. Our
  40| philosophy is to ease the difficult transition from middle school to the first year of high school by developing
  41| student’s independent skills they will require to be successful in high school. Grade eight teachers function as

===PAGE 104=== (layout, 28 lines)
   1| one inclusive team where students take classes with a variety of different teachers as they would in a high
   2| school setting. This differs from our two interdisciplinary team of teachers that have been a successful model in
   3| grades six and seven.
   4|  Lunenburg Middle School has benefited from a top notch guidance support team. A guidance counselor and a
   5| school Adjustment Counselor coupled with our shared school psychologist has been able to provide a high level
   6| of social emotional support to our students and their families. Our guidance team has been able to meet the
   7| needs of our students while preparing them to be available for academic learning.

   1|                                                     Lunenburg High School
   2|                                                        Town Report 2025
   3| Lunenburg High School and its faculty continue to focus on rigorous curriculum, high standards and
   4| opportunities for students, both academic and extracurricular, so that every student feels supported and included
   5| in our community. LHS faculty is student centered in their teaching practices, and strive to learn and to change
   6| in order to best serve all of our students.
   7|                                                         2025 School Year
   8| Lunenburg High School is rich with tradition and core values that center around student success. A talented and
   9| experienced faculty are skilled in supporting students in their learning and creating an environment that fosters
  10| independence and resilience. Our goal is for students is to acquire the skills necessary to earn a high school
  11| diploma and be successful in post-secondary education as well as in the work force.
  12| A reduction in faculty and opportunities for student choice have challenged our school community to adapt and
  13| shift to best meet the ever changing needs of the students we serve. We continue with an upward trend in both
  14| the number of students taking Advanced Placement coursework as well as the percentage of students scoring a 3
  15| or higher in those courses.
  16| We have also developed programs that support students in their daily classroom instruction. We are fortunate to
  17| have an Intervention teacher that provides direct instruction to students who were identified by their teachers as
  18| to needing additional support to be successful in the classroom. Students receive instruction in the specific class
  19| or classes they are struggling in. The data show the students participating in the intervention classroom show
  20| substantial improvement in the completion of classwork and in their overall grades.
  21|                                                         MCAS RESULTS

  28| The results indicate the LHS percentage scores for meeting and exceeding expectations are at or higher than the
  29| state average in all tested areas. In mathematics, 8 percentage points higher than the state average when
  30| compared to schools who serve students in similar grade levels.
  31| We were also very pleased to learn that 29 students at Lunenburg High School received the state’s John and
  32| Abigail Adams Scholarship this year.  The scholarship is available to students whose MCAS performance
  33| places them at the top 25 percent of their district.  To be eligible, students must either score Advanced on one
  34| exam and Proficient on the other, or Advanced on both the English and Math exams.  That is approximately 30
  35| % of grade 10 students receiving the award.

  37| Homecoming weekend was a wonderful and well attended by students, families and alumni. The weather was
  38| beautiful and highlighted the community event. The parade was a huge success with a huge turnout to support

===PAGE 108=== (plain, 43 lines)
   1| the school. Many community members noticed the care and time that were placed into the floats at each grade
   2| level.  The Blue Knights played well and won the football game and we always enjoy watching the LHMS
   3| Marching Band perform.
   4| Lunenburg High School Athletic Accomplishments
   5| Fall
   6| The golf team delivered an outstanding season, finishing 9-1 in league play and 10-1 overall in the postseason,
   7| earning the title of Mid Wach C League Champions. To cap off an exceptional year, one of our student-athletes
   8| was honored as the league MVP.
   9| The girls’ soccer team also enjoyed a remarkable season, posting an impressive league record of 8-1-3 and an
  10| overall postseason record of 13-2-3. Their consistent excellence earned them the title of Mid Wach C League
  11| Champions.
  12| The boys’ soccer team demonstrated tremendous resilience and perseverance throughout the season. While the
  13| record did not fully reflect their effort and growth, the team’s commitment to integrity and teamwork was
  14| recognized with the prestigious Sportsmanship Award for their league.
  15| The field hockey team finished in dominant fashion with an undefeated league record of 6-0-3, securing the Mid
  16| Wach C League Championship. They concluded the postseason with an outstanding 12-1-4 overall record and
  17| were further recognized by Central Mass officials for exemplary sportsmanship.
  18| The cross country program had another strong year. The girls’ team was recognized for outstanding
  19| sportsmanship in their league, while the boys’ team showed grit and determination through the final meets of
  20| the season. Two of our student-athletes were honored as Telegram & Gazette All-Stars, highlighting the
  21| program’s continued success.
  22| Football captured the Mid Wach E League Championship with an impressive 7-3 record. The team’s success
  23| was further highlighted by two student-athletes earning league MVP nominations.
  24| Cheerleading continued to build momentum this fall, earning placements at several competitions while also
  25| seeing encouraging growth in participation numbers.
  26| Unified basketball had an incredible season, culminating at the Fitchburg High School Jamboree. The event
  27| showcased the true spirit of unified athletics, as it was inspiring to see all of our student-athletes competing and
  28| celebrating together.
  29| At the middle school level, both cross country and field hockey enjoyed exciting seasons focused on skill
  30| development and growth. Coaches reported noticeable improvement and strong enthusiasm from our
  31| developing student-athletes.
  32| Winter
  33| The indoor track team has put together a tremendous season competing at both the Reggie Lewis Center and
  34| New Balance in Boston—elite venues that serve as the only sites where performances are officially recognized
  35| for meeting MIAA qualifying standards. The girls team achieved the remarkable distinction of being crowned
  36| Division 5 State Champions, while the boys team delivered an outstanding performance, finishing just behind
  37| them and placing 6th place out of 40 schools. Many hitting personal records and medaling at the meet.
  38| Boys basketball, currently holding an 11-7 record, has advanced to the finals of the Clark Tournament—one of
  39| the oldest and most respected tournaments in the country. This marks the program’s first finals appearance in 34
  40| years, with the team set to compete on February 20th. They have also secured a postseason berth as the #25 seed
  41| in Division 4.
  42| Girls basketball has also had a strong campaign, posting a 12-7 record and earning a Division 4 postseason
  43| 104

===PAGE 109=== (layout, 41 lines)
   1| berth as the #20 seed. While they fell short in the Clark Tournament, the team’s consistent play has positioned
   2| them well for tournament competition.
   3| Winter cheer made an exciting return this year for the first time in several years, and participation numbers were
   4| strong. The team has played a key role in reigniting school spirit and bringing great energy and hype to boys

  13| Our middle school basketball teams recently concluded one of their most engaging seasons to date. With many
  14| new participants and clear skill development on display at home contests, the future of Blue Knights basketball
  15| looks extremely promising as these young student-athletes continue to grow and refine their game.
  16|                                                              CURRICULUM

  18| frameworks and is rigorous and challenging. This year’s focus is to teachers will be to engage in NEASC-
  19| aligned curriculum work and unit planning to support coherent, standards-based instruction across content
  20| areas. Professional development time will be used to review, refine, and align instructional units to ensure
  21| consistency, intentional sequencing, and alignment with school wide expectations for teaching and learning.

===PAGE 112=== (layout, 46 lines)
   1|                                          As the Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School District approaches its
   2|                                          upcoming 60th  anniversary, it is apparent that our school community refuses to rest on its
   3|                                          past laurels and successes. Instead, Monty Tech continues to seek out and implement
   4|                                          innovative strategies and partnerships that will best address our diverse student body’s
   5|                                          post-secondary goals as they proceed on their workforce or educational pathways.
   6|                                          Personally, it marked my eleventh year at Monty Tech and third as its very fortunate
   7|                                          superintendent as I continue to be so appreciative of the commitment to success of our
   8|                                          students, families, instructors, staff, administrators and community partners. As always, I
   9|                                          am honored to provide our eighteen cities and towns with this annual report which
  10|                                          summarizes the District’s achievements and innovations during the 2024-2025 school
  11|                                          year.
  12| As the school year opened, Monty Tech experienced a welcome growth spurt as the District officially launched the
  13| inaugural year of the Montachusett Vocational Partnership (MVP) Academy. Created as an innovative proposal to
  14| address the building capacity issue that results in hundreds of students being deprived of the opportunity to be
  15| enrolled at Monty Tech, MVP Academy allowed nearly 80 juniors and seniors from three of our sending districts,
  16| the opportunity to receive workforce training in Electrical or House Carpentry during the school day while remaining
  17| enrolled in their sending school. Thus, as Monty Tech instructors and students worked to complete the renovation of
  18| the program’s future home, the initial MVP
  19| instruction began in an outdoor classroom
  20| located              on our main campus. As winter
  21| approached, however, the MVP students joined
  22| their Monty Tech peers to assist with the facility
  23| renovations and, in April 2025, Monty Tech
  24| welcomed dignitaries from throughout the
  25| commonwealth to simultaneously celebrate the
  26| grand opening of the MVP Academy and the
  27| graduation ceremony of the program’s first 40
  28| graduates. Looking ahead, the program hopes to
  29| expand by adding a third program, Plumbing, in                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             the
  30| fall of 2026.
  31| Of course, innovative programs like MVP Academy are not possible without the District’s efforts to alleviate the
  32| burden of costly new initiatives that could fall on the eighteen cities and towns of our regional community.
  33| Consequently, in order to avoid that scenario, 2024-2025 became noteworthy as the District’s most successful in
  34| terms of accessing competitive grants from a variety of resources. This included opportunities involving
  35| cybersecurity, equitable access, workforce training in clean energy fields and for adults with disabilities, skills
  36| capital equipment, partnership/implementation programs, no-cost adult workforce training and even anonymous
  37| corporate partner donations. In total, during the 2024-2025 school year, Monty Tech was awarded almost $3.7
  38| million in external grants and donations. Such results clearly reflect the District’s commitment to offering innovative
  39| state-of-the                                                      -art workforce training to a variety of highly skilled workers while also being mindful of the financial
  40| implications such valuable training could have on our sending communities.
  41| Without question, the MVP program represents a significant expansion of workforce training that goes beyond our
  42| annual secondary-level training efforts. However, it is important to acknowledge the ongoing efforts of our post                                                      -
  43| secondary training programs. For example, our Continuing Education program, also known as Monty Tech Nights,
  44| maintained its consecutive run of expanding enrollment across the spectrum of its offerings. Between the 2020-2021
  45| and the 2024-2025 school years, Monty Tech Nights has experienced 25-30% growth in its enrollment. An essential
  46| element of this growth has been the expanded offerings of our no-                                                                                cost training through the Career Technical

===PAGE 113=== (layout, 35 lines)
   1| Initiative (CTI). In 2024-                                                                                                                                                            2025 alone, the efforts in CTI resulted in 108 graduates in HVAC, Plumbing, Auto Body
   2| and Carpentry. Furthermore, the District, once again, applied for the most recent round of grants through CTI and
   3| was awarded the Round 10 CTI grant. Meanwhile, in June, the District’s Practical Nursing Program held its
   4| ceremonial “pinning” of 45 graduates who completed their training during the 2024-2025 school year. Monty Tech
   5| takes great pride in the fact that so many of these well-trained nurses choose to work within our local communities as
   6| nearly half of the graduates reported that they would be working for local healthcare providers including Gardner
   7| Rehabilitation, The Highlands, Fitchburg Healthcare, Athol Hospital, Dept. of Developmental Services, CAPS
   8| Collaborative, Heyward Affiliated Medical Group, MCI Gardner, Wachusett Manor and Spring Hill Recovery
   9| Center.
  10| Additionally, while expansive programs like MVP Academy, Monty Tech Nights and the Practical Nursing Program
  11| are certainly elements of our district that we take great pride in supporting, we have the same sense of pride when it
  12| comes to the small individual equipment purchases or facility renovations that happen on a year-               to-year basis. For
  13| example, during the 2024-                                                                                         2025 school year, through a variety of fiscal resources including annual Chapter 74 funds
  14| from state aid, Monty Tech introduced new appliances to our culinary program, supplemented the HVAC program’s
  15| energy efficiency equipment, installed new rooftop air conditioning equipment, replaced flooring in our student
  16| support classrooms and repaired the roof to our auditorium entry way. Such ongoing efforts to maintain a clean and
  17| safe learning environment, as well as a well-equipped instructional tool kit, are the backbone to ensuring that our
  18| students earn the industry recognized credentials and state/national SkillsUSA awards that indicate our vocational
  19| excellence. It should not be overlooked that, in 2024-2025, thanks to the wonderful support of our industry partners
  20| across the region, Monty Tech had a record-                                                  breaking year as 288 students were placed at cooperative learning sites
  21| allowing them to have real world industry training while earning money as an employee.
  22| Similarly, it is these critical efforts that allow for our consistent academic achievement as demonstrated by our
  23| MCAS Passing Rates (97% in ELA, 95% in Math and 95% in Biology) and our growing Advanced Placement
  24| results including 2024-2025 as Monty Tech experienced its highest number of AP exams administered (292), highest
  25| number of students earning a qualifying score (135) and, notably, nearly doubling the number of students who were
  26| designated AP Scholars for earning a qualifying score on three different AP exams (35).
  27| To conclude, while it is clear that there will be changes to traditional vocational school operations across the
  28| Commonwealth, Monty Tech will continue to focus on overall student achievement, outstanding instructional
  29| practice and the support for our sending communities. Without question, as an institution, we take great pride in the
  30| numerous achievements highlighted in this annual report, but we additionally acknowledge that our success as a
  31| school is dependent on the ongoing support of the civic leadership and residents of our eighteen communities.
  32| On behalf of everyone at Monty Tech, we are grateful for that continued support and greatly value the opportunity to
  33| be an educational partner to all of our communities.
  34| Respectfully submitted,
  35| Thomas R. Browne, Superintendent-Director

===PAGE 115=== (layout, 17 lines)
   1| Each year, Monty Tech’s Business Manager works in conjunction with the Superintendent and 22-                       member
   2| School Committee, to develop a cost-effective budget that reflects the values and priorities of the institution.
   3| The final fiscal year 2024-                               2025 Educational Plan totaled $33,334,174 which represented a modest 2.46%
   4| increase over the 2023-2024 Educational Plan.  Remarkably, Monty Tech has been able to deliver highly
   5| effective, meaningful academic and vocational training programs, operating on one of the Commonwealth’s
   6| more conservative budgets.  In fact, the FY25 budget exceeded the minimum spending required by
   7| Massachusetts General Law Chapter 70 by only 0.8%, while other Massachusetts vocational school districts
   8| operated on budgets that exceeded the FY25 Required Net School Spending by as much as 65%.  Further, a
   9| historical review of district expenses confirms a commitment to provide resources where they benefit
  10| students most – instruction.
  11| While we are proud to offer vital education and training programs at a minimal cost to our member
  12| communities, we understand that vocational education is, in fact, more costly than a traditional,
  13| comprehensive academic program.  To that end, school officials pursue countless grant opportunities to
  14| expand and improve training programs each year.   For the fiscal year 2025, state and federal grant sources
  15| provided the district with $4,728,144.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Programs funded by these grants include: Special Education Services
  16| and Program Improvement, Title I Support, Perkins Occupational Education, Vocational Capital Equipment
  17| Enhancements, Student Support and Academic Enrichment, and No-Cost Evening Training Initiatives.

   7| While Monty Tech’s academic programs continue to evolve, the district maintains a strong commitment to
   8| equity and access by intentionally supporting and honoring the language proficiency of our multilingual
   9| students. Monty Tech is a proud participant in the Massachusetts State Seal of
  10| Biliteracy program, which recognizes multilingualism as an asset and promotes
  11| equitable access to postsecondary and career opportunities for English Learners.
  12| In its inaugural year of participation, Monty Tech demonstrated strong outcomes.

  15| Distinction in Haitian Creole. Overall, 77% of test takers earned the Seal, reflecting
  16| a high level of language proficiency among participating students. In addition, a
  17| Monty Tech staff member earned the Seal of Biliteracy with Distinction in Spanish, further modeling the
  18| value of multilingualism within our school community.
  19| This DESE-           recognized credential affirms students’ attainment of high levels of English proficiency
  20| alongside another language, strengthens college and career readiness, and enhances students’
  21| competitiveness in the workforce and global economy. Monty Tech remains committed to providing English
  22| Learners with inclusive, standards-aligned instruction and multiple pathways to demonstrate mastery, while
